speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
that Bill C-51, an Act to prohibit the advertising and promotion and respecting the labelling and monitoring of tobacco products, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-51 now before the House addresses the issue of current tobacco marketing practices. Its effect would be to ban the advertising of tobacco products available for sale in Canada. It would also ban tobacco product promotion and regulate labelling and the reporting of technical information.
The federal Government has taken an active role in addressing the issue of cigarette smoking. It is important for people to understand why smoking, which was thought of as merely a personal habit, has become a legitimate public concern. There is overwhelming evidence that tobacco smoke is the largest preventable cause of illness, disability and premature death in Canada. Moreover, it has also become evident that Canadians who are consistently exposed to smoke in the environment may suffer from adverse health effects. Not surprisingly, the public is increasingly asking for an environment that protects non-smokers from tobacco smoke.
[DOT] (M10)
As Minister of National Health and Welfare, my primary concern is the health of Canadians. Therefore, I must do all that I can to protect their health by discouraging the advertising and promotion of tobacco, and by increasing public health knowledge of the health hazards of smoking.
This is not a moral crusade. It is not a case of some overzealous individuals attempting to force their life-style on others. It is responsible government action in reaction to overwhelming evidence that tobacco, despite its widespread use by a third of the adult population, is actually responsible for nearly 100 deaths a day in Canada.
The health risks of tobacco were realized long after it had become an established industry and millions of Canadians had become dependent. If tobacco were discovered tomorrow, no government would permit its sale, let alone its advertising. No one is immune, since scientific studies have revealed that nonsmokers can be harmed in a smoke polluted environment.
Each year tobacco prematurely kills Canadians. On average, one Canadian dies of smoke related illness every 17 minutes of every day. I ask the rhetorical question, do Canadians, and those who may have some hesitation about this form of legislation, not have a right to expect that a Minister of health and a Parliament has a duty to face those facts? Victims are obviously mostly smokers, but some are non-smokers, and they are Canadians of all ages.
At least 500,000 Canadians have died prematurely of tobacco related illnesses since 1964. I choose that year because it was in that year that the Surgeon General of the United States first published the link between cigarette smoking and death. About one-quarter of deaths among people aged 35 to 84 in 1985 could be attributed to smoking. Today, smoking continues to be the leading cause of preventable death in Canada.
Tobacco is not a consumer product like any other widely advertised product on the market. Tobacco, a toxic and addictive substance, is the only consumer product that is dangerous when used exactly as intended. There simply is no level of safe smoking.
Of 23 known human carcinogens, 6 are components of tobacco smoke. Tobacco smoke also contains dozens of other chemicals that are toxic to humans. Tobacco is such a highly addictive substance that the vast majority of individuals who smoke are unable to limit their intake, even if they are aware of the health risks and would like to quit. Only 30 per cent of tobacco users manage to break their addiction, although polls show that more than 80 per cent would like to do so.
Some killer connections, like lung cancer and emphysema, are reasonably well known. However, many Canadians, especially the many teenagers who smoke, do not realize that heart disease is actually the leading cause of death among smokers. Almost no one knows that gangrene and amputations result from some tobacco caused peripheral vascular diseases.
November 23, 1987

Few know that in terms of over-all mortality and death rates, low tar, low nicotine cigarettes appear to be only slightly less hazardous than high tar, high nicotine brands.
In 1969, an all-Party committee of the House of Commons concluded that there was no longer any scientific controversy regarding the risk created by cigarette smoking. But it stated that the tobacco industry, by refusing to accept the established medical evidence, was directly responsible for causing confusion and delays. That was stated in 1969 by an all-Party committee of this House, and I would suggest that the same remains today.
Action is long overdue. A Private Member's Bill, Bill C-204, is further action in this House in respect to this legislation. We do not need more studies. We do not need more dead and disabled bodies. We need immediate action, including preventive educational campaigns and concrete efforts to strip tobacco of its alluring image.
Accordingly, on April 30, I tabled in the House of Commons Bill C-51, the Tobacco Products Control Act, and today it is here for second reading. The main provisions contained in the Bill are the following. First, with respect to advertising promotion of tobacco products, a ban on the advertising of tobacco products sold in Canada; a prohibition of the use of the brand name of a tobacco product or its trade mark, in any promotion of tobacco companies sponsorship or other support for any activity event, publication or broadcast; the prohibition of any free distribution of tobacco products; the prohibition of any gifts or cash rebates or the right to participate in contests, lotteries, or games related to the proof of purchase of a tobacco product; and prohibition of the use of a tobacco product brand name or trade mark on any non-tobacco goods that may be used to promote the sale of the product.
Second, with respect to labelling of tobacco products, a requirement that tobacco product packages display, on a rotating basis, a series of new, stronger, more visible health warnings; a requirement that packages also display a listing of toxic constituents found in tobacco products or tobacco smoke, including levels of tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide; and a restriction on the use of writing on tobacco product packages to the name, brand name, and any trade marks of the tobacco product and information specifically required by this and any other relevant legislation.
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, and I know that it does not include you, whether Members of the House have recently looked at a tobacco product and read the warning. The warning is totally inconsequential. Keep in mind that it is on a tobacco package. What the Minister of National Health and Welfare is warning the purchaser and the user to do, when he or she uses the product, is to avoid inhaling. That is how weak the message is today.
Third, with respect to reporting of tobacco related information to the Government, a requirement that constituents specified by regulations and their quantities, in the tobacco product itself or the smoke produced from it, be reported; and
Tobacco Products
a requirement that tobacco product production, import and sales information also be provided.
In the Bill there are also effective dates. I know that implementation of those dates will need adjustment, and that will be an examination to which the legislative committee will have to give close consideration.
My decision to introduce those strong and comprehensive legislative measures to control tobacco products came following much thoughtful consideration. After examining the evidence that has accumulated on the effects of tobacco and tobacco smoke, I came to the conclusion that continued advertising and promotion of a product which is so clearly hazardous and addictive poses a significant threat to public health that is no longer acceptable. Tobacco use has become a national public health problem of pressing and substantial concern.
The effects of direct exposure to tobacco have been clearly demonstrated over the past decades. Approximately 35,000 Canadians die prematurely each year from smoke-related diseases. Smoking contributes to some 30 per cent of cancer deaths, 30 per cent of heart disease deaths, and 85 per cent of chronic obstructive lung disease deaths.
Moreover, we have become increasingly concerned that smoking is a health hazard to non-smokers. Those who share indoor space with smokers can be placed at health risk, particularly when they are exposed for long periods of time.
A report of the U.S. Surgeon General recently concluded that involuntary smoking "is a cause of disease including lung cancer in healthy non-smokers". I am pleased today to add that an expert committee here in Canada, which convened at the request of my Department, has also completed a review of the world-wide evidence on this matter. In its report entitled "Involuntary Exposure to Tobacco Smoke", it concluded that the chronic inhalation of environmental tobacco smoke by nonsmokers is associated with increased risk of various diseases including lung cancer. The expert committee also reported that all available scientific evidence on passive smoking is consistent with policies which eliminate all involuntary exposure.
These statistics on smoking in Canada indicate the existence of a serious health problem and suggest certain disturbing trends. Currently Canada ranks as one of the top 10 countries in the world in per capita consumption of cigarettes. A Gallup poll conducted in May of 1985 showed that 34 per cent of Canadians 18 years of age and over smoke cigarettes. While the proportion of smokers in Canada has been slowly decreasing, the number of young Canadian women smoking continues to increase. Among Canadian women in their twenties the proportion of daily smokers increased from 36 per cent in 1983 to 45 per cent in 1986. While we see the trends in general going down, among Canadian women we see the trend going up.

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
Obviously we are concerned about various cancers, especially young women and breast cancer. Today the rate of lung cancer among Canadian women is almost equal to that of breast cancer. I ask Canadians in a very straightforward manner whether they expect their Minister of Health, their Government, and their Parliament to be silent in the face of that type of evidence.
I would suggest that Parliament is trying to catch up with public opinion on the issue. Moreover, smoking rates remain high for young people, many of whom start to smoke even before reaching their teenage years. The onset of regular smoking often takes place as early as age 12. By age 18 to 19, 37 per cent of young people are smoking daily. The facts that so many teenagers continue to smoke daily and that young women are now smoking more suggest that the recent over-all decline in cigarette sales may be offset in the near future by increases brought about by a new generation of smokers.
The decision to start smoking is not an informed choice. It is a decision precipitated by what young people perceive to be the social acceptability and desirability of tobacco use. Sophisticated and well-targeted tobacco advertising has much to do with creating powerful and appealing images of the lifestyle of a smoker. To minimize any potential health concerns young people may have, ads have been cleverly designed to show healthy looking, physically active smokers enjoying their workout in the gym, taking to the ski slopes, bicycling in the clean outdoors, and in general staying trim and keeping fit. These ads are not designed to impart factual information about tobacco products or the consequence of their use.
Just recently in the British Journal of Addictions there are some interesting statistics to indicate that children at a very early age are able to identify brand names with advertising. I will not go into those statistics today, but we find indications that children under the age of 10 years can already identify brand names with the ads.
1 wish to make another point which I stated to some ad executives the other day. Is the advertising industry of Canada, in spending S75 million on tobacco ads, so inefficient that that $75 million does not convince one Canadian to try the product? Yet, they turn around and argue "give us your account and we will sell your product". Why does it work with every product except tobacco?
The public has certainly become more concerned about tobacco advertising and promotion since the sponsorship of the R. J. R. Macdonald Tobacco company of the Canadian Ski Association in 1983, ad campaigns which were directed toward recruiting new smokers among Canadian youth. The manufacturers claim that their sole purpose in advertising is to promote brand switching among current smokers. However, in view of the fact that smoking habits are generally established by age 20, it is not surprising that there is the temptation to engage in tobacco marketing activities targeted at youth.
Currently the Canadian Tobacco Manufacturers Council has a code to regulate voluntarily the advertising and promotion practices of member companies. While the code is partially restricted to tobacco advertising, the rules are weak and many of them have been violated.
In response to the concerns regarding tobacco advertising and promotion, I have on a number of occasions met with representatives of the Canadian Tobacco Manufacturers Council over the past few years. On the whole these discussions have failed to persuade me that a voluntary selfregulating approach to advertising is workable.
The purpose of tobacco advertising is to encourage over-all tobacco use. The advertiser hopes that it will also encourage the use of his particular brand. Alternatively it is the policy of the Government to discourage tobacco use. Since these objectives are mutually incompatible, the Government has concluded that legislation banning all tobacco product advertising is the only acceptable option.
There is a strong national consensus calling for action. Public opinion polls indicate that a majority of Canadians favour measures similar to those proposed here. In 1987, 67 per cent of those expressing an opinion supported the proposal of the federal Government to ban tobacco advertising, which was an increase from 62 per cent in 1986. In 1979, 80 per cent favoured federal legislation for health warnings and toxic substances reporting on packages. This consensus in favour of action supports the national movement toward non-smoking, which is getting stronger.
I say to my colleagues in the House that health is not a partisan issue. While the Government is generally supportive of health regulation, this is not the case where products have serious health consequences. The challenge facing us is to regulate in such a manner as to protect public health and safety while imposing the fewest restrictions possible on individual freedoms.
Let me say a few words about freedom of speech, a freedom treasured by all of us in the House. Freedom of speech must be accompanied by the responsible exercise of that freedom. Freedom and responsibility are like two sides of the same coin; they are inseparable. Many Canadians believe that the responsible exercise of freedom of speech does not include the freedom to advertise addictive products. The responsible exercise of freedom of speech does not include the freedom to portray a lethal product as glamorous and socially acceptable. It does not include the freedom to advertise and promote addictive lethal products which can be easily obtained by teenagers and even younger children.
I submit that tobacco advertising conducted in exactly these ways represents the exercise of freedom without responsibility. One-sided coins are being spread around the community purporting to represent freedom of speech. There is a tail side of alleged free speech, but the coins have no head side of social responsibility. This coinage is worthless; it is without value.
November 23, 1987

Prohibiting the sale of a social drug like tobacco is not feasible, but prohibiting the advertising and promotion of this toxic substance is both feasible and desirable. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms provides for reasonable limits on our freedoms including freedom of speech. Since the evidence shows tobacco use to be a public health problem of pressing and national concern, a complete ban on tobacco promotion is consistent with a responsible health policy under our Constitution. By outlawing tobacco advertising, the federal Government is conveying a clear, unequivocal message-tobacco is a dangerous substance.
The advertising ban is but only a part, although a key part, of a long term comprehensive health oriented policy on tobacco and smoking. The long term objective is to bring about a significant decline in smoking and tobacco consumption. An essential tool for meeting this objective is the national program to reduce tobacco use, a joint effort of provincial, territorial and the federal Governments plus major health organizations. In the short term, the Government's objectives are to strengthen the existing trend against the social acceptability of smoking and to enhance the credibility of the health message.
I am speaking today not only to parliamentarians but to the country and to those who are parents, relatives and close friends of children and young adults whose actions can now determine the quality and duration of their later life. To replace smokers who quit or die prematurely, the tobacco industry annually must attract many new smokers. Virtually all of these replacement smokers are children or adolescents. Tobacco purchases by children and adolescents exceed $250 million every year. While older Canadians are quitting the tobacco habit in record numbers, smoking among teenagers has not decreased.
Voluntary controls on tobacco advertising have been tried without success in Canada, and more than 15 years of experience with the Canadian Tobacco Manufacturers Council voluntary code, including well documented breaches of both the spirit and the letter of its provisions, have resulted in a loss of public confidence in this approach.
Violations of virtually every rule of the voluntary code have been reported. Rule 11 prohibiting outdoor cigarette advertising adjacent to schools has been frequently flaunted. Cigarette brands have been launched with blatant appeals to youth. Health warnings which are supposed to be permanently displayed are often virtually invisible on billboards and in print ads, so we have stepped up our efforts to communicate health concerns about tobacco to Canadians, especially through increased support of the national program to reduce tobacco use.
The presence of massive amounts of tobacco product promotions, however, simply dwarfs efforts to communicate the health hazards of smoking. Simply stated, many people just do not take health warnings seriously when they are
Tobacco Products
bombarded at every turn of the head with soothing tobacco company ads promoting their product as normal, good and glamorous.
I would suggest the young are particularly vulnerable to such appeal. Young people are also good hypocrisy detectors. Tobacco ads prominently displayed at every corner store make government health warnings ring hollow. As long as glossy advertising campaigns lure young persons into thinking that smoking is okay, our society will continue to pay an unconscionable price in premature deaths and disabilities. Tobacco advertising fosters social acceptability of a dangerous product. The ability of the tobacco industry to stay healthy while its customers get sick is, according to a recent report in a business magazine cover story, "One of the most amazing marketing feats of all times".
I also want to assure Members of the House and all Canadians that the measures we are discussing are not intended to prohibit smoking in Canada. That is another argument that opponents to this legislation have said it provides for. Cigarettes have been used in Canada since the turn of the century and other tobacco products for a lot longer than that. Tobacco use has been legal too long to consider such measures. It is my intention and my hope that the Bill will continue to reduce smoking.
As well when Bill C-51 was made public other anti-smoking measures were announced, intended to strike a balance between legislative and program initiatives. By combining legislation, education, restrictions on smoking in indoor environments and transitional assistance to tobacco growers, the Government has developed a comprehensive and balanced policy to reduce the tragic consequences of smoking on our society.
For my part, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that on April 22 I announced my commitment to strengthen significantly my Department's participation in the national program to reduce tobacco smoking. This national program, launched in 1985, was established to unite provincial, territorial and federal Governments and national health organizations in co-ordinated action toward a common purpose, that of developing effective and comprehensive initiatives to reduce the use of tobacco in Canada.
We have three goals: one, to protect the health and rights of non-smokers; two, to help non-smokers stay smoke free; and three, to encourage and help those who want to quit smoking. The initial focus of the national program through the "Break Free for a New Generation of Non-Smokers" campaign has been directed at youth at the vulnerable ages of 12 to 17. In support of the national effort, the Department of National Health and Welfare has developed and is now promoting the implementation of a school based smoking prevention program for Grade 6. We are also completing work on two other educational resources, a guide book of project ideas for community youth groups such as YM-YWCA's boys and girls clubs and a smoke-free educational kit for children aged three

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
to six for use in day care settings and kindergarten classes. Provinces and health agencies have also tied some of their own activities into the national program, including, for example, New Brunswick's "Business for Kids" projects and Alberta's publication on women and smoking called "Break Free- Leaving the Pack Behind."
Other concerns to be addressed through the program include promoting the benefits of a smoke free life among our youth and helping them to deal with peer and other social pressures to smoke; reversing the increasing trend in smoking among young women; increasing the accessibility of effective cessation programs; supporting the initiatives of community groups responding to local needs, and ensuring that all Canadians have the opportunity to grow up, live and work in healthy smoke free environments.
Several federal departments have restricted smoking on the job. These include my own department, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, the Auditor General's Office, the National Research Council, the Public Service Commission, Statistics Canada and others. On April 22, my colleague, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) announced new measures, both short and long term, to restrict smoking in workplaces subject to federal jurisdiction. In the short term, the Minister of Labour is requesting employers to restrict smoking in their workplaces to designated areas by the end of 1987. Also on the same day, the then President of the Treasury Board, now the Minister of State (Science and Technology) (Mr. Oberle), announced the Government's intention to ban smoking in all public service workplaces by January 1, 1989. In August, we reaffirmed our intention by announcing that for a 15 month period beginning October 1, 1987, smoking throughout the public service was to be restricted to specifically designated areas. I know this is not ideal, but I think it is a very big step forward.
As well, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that I recently wrote to you outlining my concerns about the health hazards of involuntary smoking and the need to control exposure to tobacco smoke within the precincts of the Parliament of Canada. Similar letters were sent to the Speaker of the Senate and the parliamentary librarian. I am happy to report to this House that both Speakers and the parliamentary librarian responded quickly and positively to my concerns. At their request, a committee of officials of both Houses of Parliament and the Parliamentary Library have been meeting to draw up alternative strategies for the control of tobacco use that would apply to all locations occupied by the Parliament of Canada. It is my hope that the policy adopted will be comparable to the approach taken elsewhere in federal jurisdiction.
The House will recall also that last November the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) proposed a new air regulation to ban smoking in Canadian aircraft for domestic and trans border flight segments of less than two hours. If Members of Parliament look back at what people have been telling them as they have been flying to and from their ridings, they will agree that comments from the public have been overwhelmingly
favourable. Accordingly, these new regulations will be fully implemented by Canadian airlines before the end of this year.
I recognize as well that with these changes, difficulties can occur for those in the industry. Recognizing the serious difficulties faced by tobacco farmers as demand for their products declines, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced the establishment of an alternative enterprise-initiated program to assist diversification in the tobacco growing regions of Canada. On April 23, in conjuction with the Ontario Agriculture and Food Minister, details of a $30 million program to assist Ontario farmers who cease tobacco production was announced, the funding of which will be shared equally by the two orders of Government.
The legislation the House is now debating has been misinterpreted in many areas. Tobacco has not been singled out for legislation; nor is it a precendent-setting exercise. Intervention to regulate dangerous or potentially dangerous products and to reduce or prevent problems is considered an appropriate role of Government in Canada. Prescription drugs, for instance, may not be advertised to the general public. Alcohol which is harmful if used in excess is already regulated both provincially and federally. If it is legally and socially acceptable to prohibit some forms of advertising, I believe we should have no qualms about prohibiting any form of advertising for the nation's leading cause of preventable death.
It is not true, as the tobacco industry claims, that ad bans in other countries have been unsuccessful. In counties where tobacco advertising has been effectively banned, consumption has remained stable and at lower levels than in Canada. Bans have been in effect since the mid 1970s in Norway and Finland. Per person consumption rates in those two countries are 50 per cent lower than in Canada. In the five years following the tobacco advertising ban in Norway, cigarette sales declined by 15 per cent with the largest component of the decline being among children and particularly girls.
If that is not sufficient evidence, we only need note what the Government of China announced last week. China is a society that is heavily into the practice of smoking. It is very interesting to see a country like China taking the lead from the World Health Organization and taking the steps that are beginning to be taken in respect to the use of this product.
Education and legislation are both important. By pursuing these complementary approaches and by working together, I am confident that we can achieve the mutually beneficial goal of a smoke-free society. In a world where private gain ranks supreme, we must not lose sight of the need to work for the indivisible social benefits that come from the pursuit of public health objectives.
If this Bill passes this stage, it will go to the legislative committee. There members of the committee will have the responsibility to decide whether the specific provisions of this Bill are reasonable and effective. They will have to look at the
November 23, 1987

issue in light of the evidence that I have presented today. 1 look forward to seeing the judgment of the legislative committee.
I believe that a smoke-free environment is as essential to human health as pasteurized milk and chlorinated water. Sooner or later, every country will ban tobacco advertising and promotion in an effort to combat the greatest man-made epidemic of modern times. Canada has the opportunity to set an important example for the rest of the world in the effective control of this critical public health problem. The decision rests with each one of us as to whether we are willing to take an active, pro-health stand or whether we are willing to defend the indefensible in the face of the evidence I have produced today.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to point out that I believe that all of us in the House of Commons today are guilty of a bit of hypocrisy in introducing this particular piece of legislation. The laudable objective of this legislation is to cut down on the consumption of cigarette and other kinds of tobacco in Canada. We all know, and we have heard the statistics from the Minister, that a cigarette is an instrument of death. However, I do not see any political party actually calling for a ban on cigarettes.
We are saying that tobacco is a hazardous product, a product responsible for thousands of preventable deaths in Canada. We are saying that it is a product which costs the health care system millions. Yet if we were to carry that argument to its ultimate conclusion, we as parliamentarians would actually vote on a Bill to ban the sale of tobacco products in Canada. However, no political party has the courage to do that.
We realize that tobacco has been a part of our culture for many hundreds of years. We realize that the negative health effects of tobacco have become evident only in the last number of years. Yet frankly, from a strict political point of view, I do not think any political party would want to go into the next election trumpeting itself as the party which will introduce prohibition on tobacco. That is a fact.
If we are stopping short of actually banning the sale of this hazardous product, what steps are we prepared to take to cut down on its use over the next number of years? Certainly, a ban on tobacco advertising is one strategy which is supportable in the move to cut down on the consumption of tobacco. However, I think there is a more fundamental principle which unfortunately the Minister did not address.
Just a few moments ago I had delivered to my desk from the legislative assistant to the Minister a summary of the expert committee report on involuntary exposure to tobacco smoke. This particular report indicates that chronic inhalation of environmental tobacco smoke, other people's smoke, is associated with an increased risk of lung cancer and that ETS probably causes lung cancer. An expert committee has made an analysis which shows that those who do not smoke but work
Tobacco Products
in a place where they are exposed to environmental smoke may have an increased risk of lung cancer.
While the Minister has introduced legislation specifically designed to deal with advertising, he has not dealt with the more fundamental right of Canadians to live and work in a smoke-free environment. The Minister has mentioned that certain initiatives will be undertaken by regulations which relate to federal Government employees, and that is to be lauded. However, there are literally millions of Canadians who live and work in places which are not covered by regulations that apply only to civil servants.
The Government is saying that it believes civil servants should have the right to work in a smoke-free environment, but what about the thousands of other employees working under federal jurisdiction who will not necessarily see any benefit arising from this legislation because there are no fines or ways of enforcing companies under federal jurisdiction which do not live up to the requirement to provide a smoke-free workplace? The employees of banks, trucking companies and other companies involved in interprovincial transport will see no respite from second-hand smoke as a result of this legislation.
More important are the millions of Canadians who work at the provincial level and are covered by provincial legislation. This Bill does nothing to provide a smoke-free work environment for the millions of Canadians who should have the right to work in a smoke-free environment.
In a small way, this legislation touches upon the future tobacco consumption pattern of teenagers and young people. Representatives from the Canadian Cancer Society who are here in the gallery today certainly see this as being a step in the right direction. It is a step in the direction of cutting down on the increasing numbers of young people who are seduced into the world of smoking as the result of things like kiddy packs, which are still legal, and advertisements which show that those who smoke are part of the gang, part of the attractive culture of young people who are in style.
Certainly this measure will deal with that in a small way. However, even if one accepts that this Bill does not address a major flaw, which means millions of Canadians will continue to have to breathe second-hand smoke for at least eight hours a day, which by the Minister's own study released today could cause them to contract cancer, we should take a few moments to look at the Bill as it relates to advertising and point out just how flawed it really is.
Many of us have been involved in the debate in this Chamber over the last number of weeks concerning the Mulroney trade deal. I submit that as a result of that deal, this legislation will do nothing to prevent the advertising of tobacco products in Canada. I will tell you why. It is quite simple.
One item on the table under the heading "Services" is printing. We know that if and when the final deal is signed, it

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
will be possible for Canadian companies to go to the U.S. and have their material printed there. Let us take, for example, tobacco advertisements which have been a rather significant portion of revenue for Canadian magazine publishing companies. All those companies have to do to get around this law is to have their magazines printed in the U.S. and then sold back in Canada. If it is published in the U.S. it is not a Canadian magazine and therefore not subject to Canadian regulations governing advertising.
If the Minister really wants to bring in legislation to ban all tobacco advertising in Canada, he has to recognize that the ban should be applied equally to magazines and other reading material coming from outside the country. I do not think he wants to inadvertently introduce legislation to encourage Canadian magazines to go south of the border to be printed, so amendments have to be made. There is no point in spending a lot of time discussing this issue in this House if as soon as the trade deal is completed the Canadian publisher just turns around and has his magazine printed in the United States in order to be exempt from Canadian laws on tobacco advertising.
There is another major flaw dealing with trade marks. The Minister has stated that if a company wants to sponsor, for example, a sporting or cultural event, it can use only its corporate name. It cannot use the brand name of a cigarette or even chewing tobacco, which we know has not been addressed in this legislation. All the company has to do in order to get around this provision is to register all its brand names as corporate names.
For example, if you want to have a du Maurier Special or Player's International Tournament, for a few hundred dollars you can put together a corporation under those names and get around this law. The law does not prohibit tobacco companies from sponsoring-
You do not know what you are talking about.

I am not sure of his riding but the Hon. Member asks, "What is the Member talking about?". He made a comment about the U.S.S.R. during the Minister's remarks and I thought that was rather interesting. However, if he has read the legislation-
I know a hell of a lot more about it than you do.

Then he should be aware of Clause 5(1) under "Promotion":
-no person shall employ the brand name or a trade mark of a tobacco product in any representation made to the public for the purpose of acknowledging financial or other support provided by a manufacturer-
I suppose the Hon. Member has not read this far, but Clause 5(2) states quite categorically:
Notwithstanding section 3, the name of a manufacturer or importer of tobacco products may be used in a representation referred to in subsection
(D-
Quite clearly, if a company wants to advertise the Player's International, all it would have to do is incorporate a Player's International company. That would permit it to continue to advertise. The Minister knows that is true. When I was lobbied by the tobacco company, I pointed to this flaw. You know what the tobacco company said? We want to live within the spirit of the law. They also said they will live within the law as it is written. Knowing their record for not moving on voluntary bans or restrictions on advertising, they will use every loophole at their disposal to get their message out. Those loopholes include incorporating new companies and having their material printed south of the border. Unless we move amendments to address these concerns, the tobacco companies will continue to advertise in some way, shape or form in Canada.
There is another major flaw in this legislation. The Minister was right when he pointed out the disturbing consumption patterns among young people, in particular young women, as they relate to tobacco advertising. We know it is illegal for children under the age of 16 to purchase tobacco products. We also know from testimony with respect to Bill C-204 that the average age a person begins smoking is 12. How are they getting their cigarettes? They may be getting them through stores. We have had evidence to show that nine times out of 10 they can buy them directly from the corner store even though it is illegal. However, there is another way to get them with absolutely no prohibition, and that is through vending machines.
In his legislation the Minister addresses vending machines, but not to make them illegal, which seems to me to be the logical consequence of the statement that young people are smoking at a greater rate in greater numbers and earlier than ever before. Why has the Minister not introduced a ban on vending machines? What he has done is set out regulations on advertising on vending machines. How can the Minister justify his intention to allow the continued growth of vending machines when he knows they are one sure fire way for children to get cigarettes? When a six-year old puts, I guess, three "Loons" in a vending machine he or she gets a package of cigarettes in the same way a 60-year old does. Quite clearly if the Minister is committed to reducing consumption among juveniles, one way of doing that is through a ban on vending machines, which is not contained in this legislation.

read into the record a letter which was sent out by the Member for Willowdale. He calls this piece of legislation a form of censorship which has no place in our free market society. He sent this letter to the President of Ted Bates Advertising Inc. It reads:
The thrust of Bill C-51 is to curb the social acceptability of smoking

The total ban on tobacco however, is a form of censorship which has no place in our free-market society.
It is not the role of the government to selectively decide what commercial messages may be heard by the population. The letter goes on:
I will be approaching the Minister to reconsider his proposed legislation on banning all tobacco advertising, for I sincerely felt that this action represents an intervention in the marketplace which threatens individuals and commercial freedoms.
Hear, hear.

He sure does.

The letter concludes:

Once again, thank you for taking the time to inform me of your opinion on this subject. Best wishes and warm regards.
I would not have read this letter into the record had the Member for Willowdale not somehow suggested to me that the solution to this problem lies with the provincial Government of Ontario when he has promised the advertisers that he personally will go to the Minister of Health and will personally move to stop this Bill.
Yet, we have been threatened by the Government that if we put up too many speakers on this legislation the Government will drop the Bill and will blame it on the Opposition. That is because the government Minister involved does not want to let his Members loose to speak their minds about this piece of legislation. He wants a cosy little deal and I can understand why.
I have other letters. If the Member would like I will read some letters which other members of the Conservative Party sent out in out in opposition to this Bill.
I have tried to point out what I consider to be a number of flaws in the Bill which I believe will neuter the Bill and render it impotent in what I consider to be the main objectives, that of providing a smoke-free environment for Canadians. The first is guaranteeing a smoke-free workplace and the second is cutting down on consumption by strategies including a ban on advertising.
I think that a ban on advertising is completely defensible. 1 agree with the Minister that there are many other instances

where, as a part of public policy, we have introduced restrictions. 1 think, for example, of the restrictions which have been introduced with regard to the advertising of pharmaceutical products. I think of the voluntary ban on the advertising of distilled spirits which was entered into under the threat of legislation. There are certainly many instances where the Government has deemed, whether as a result of a voluntary ban or public policy, that certain messages are not good to be transmitted through the media.
I also admit that in the support of this legislation we in this House are all guilty of hypocrisy because we are not prepared to take the full step of a total ban. However, from the point of view of societal norms I do not believe that that is a possibility at this time.
The Member on the government side likened this piece of legislation to measures in the U.S.S.R. I think he did so because he has concerns about some of his constituents. When the first legislation on this issue was introduced last April we did not hear very much about alternative funding for the tobacco farmers who are being driven out of business as a result of decreasing consumption of tobacco and will certainly be further affected by this legislation. I was happy to hear the Minister make some mention in his speech today to some transitional funding for them which we have to consider.
We must also consider the role of the Government in offering transitional funding for sports and cultural organizations which could be adversely affected by corporate requirements to move away from their sponsorship. I believe that the Government must address that issue in tandem with this legislation.
Madam Speaker, I think that as far as the smoking problem is concerned, what we as Members of this House have to decide today is whether we want to adopt strategies that will lead to a reduction in the consumption of tobacco in Canada. If we wanted to be really thorough about this, and I think all Parties would agree, we would have to ban the sale of tobacco products in Canada, but we know that is not possible. It is impossible because smoking has been part of our culture for thousands of years.
No, no, no!

I knew 1 would be corrected by my hon. colleague who knows far more about the subject than I do. I am looking forward to her comments.
In any case, smoking has been ingrained in our society for quite some time, and not one political party would have the courage today to make banning the sale of tobacco in Canada part of its political platform in the next election. That would be hardly likely.

What we must do as Members is, first of all, give Canadians a working environment where they will not be exposed to smoke produced by others. According to a report released today by the Minister's office, people who work in environments where there is a great deal of smoke are more likely to get cancer. I think the primary purpose of any Bill of this kind should be to guarantee Canadians a smoke-free environment at work. That we do not find in this document, and we do not find it because the Minister prefers to proceed by regulating federal employees. That is fine for federal workers, but many people working in the private sector or even the federal level will not be entitled to a smoke-free environment because the regulations do not even impose fines on companies that refuse to provide such an environment for their employees.
If I happen to work in a small transport company or bank and I want to claim the right to work in a smoke-free environment, I can't because there is not even a mechanism to apply the regulations. And that is one of the flaws in this Bill.
