Thank you, Madam Speaker. The House is aware that under this Canada-US deal, printing is defined as a service, which creates a situation in view of the fact that this Bill refers specifically to magazines which are published by Canadians in Canada. Since magazines such as Maclean's or Chatelaine may be printed in the United States, as a result of the Canada-US deal and then be imported into Canada, they could therefore still contain tobacco advertising. In this case, if we are really serious about prohibiting the advertising and promotion of tobacco products in Canada, we should propose amendments to this Bill to really cover all magazines sold in Canada, whether imported or printed here, failing which, Madam Speaker, when the provisions of the Canada-US deal authorize accross-the-border printing within the next two years, tobacco manufactures will be able to pressure Canadian publishers into having their magazines sold here but printed in
the United States, thereby avoiding the regulations which will result from this Bill.
On the other hand, since this Bill will only prohibit the trade mark use of a product with sports events, for instance, they will be able to refer to the Imperial Tobacco Races or the Imperial Competition; they would not be able to refer to the Players Competition, because Players now is the trade mark of a product. To bypass the provisions of Bill C-51, companies need only introduce such names as Players Inc. or DuMaurier Inc. It is a well known fact that for a few hundred dollars, a company may be incorporated in Canada under another name and thus not fall within the scope of this Bill.
It has other deficiencies. The minister himself emphasized that the purpose of this Bill was to reduce tobacco consumption among children and teenagers, for adults have come to realize the detrimental effects of tobacco and there has been a marked decline in tobacco use among them. But among teenagers, partly because of advertising and partly because of peer pressure, there has been an abnormal increase in tobacco consumption, especially among young women; if the minister really wants to prevent an increase of tobacco use among teenagers, I suggest the Bill should also prohibit all cigarette vending machines in Canada. As you know, Madam Speaker, it is already illegal to sell cigarettes to young people under 16 years of age; while some stores will sell them cigarettes, others will not. But if there is a cigarette vending machine, and if I am seven years old with three quarters in my pockets- nowadays it is more like three dollars-but that was the case quite a long time ago.
A seven-year old with three dollars' worth of change can get cigarettes the same as a sixty-year-old. I think the Minister also should have banned vending machine sales, to make sure that the young will not be able to obtain cigarettes outside convenience stores and that the latter are more strictly regulated with respect to the sale of tobacco to minors.
It is common knowledge, and we were told by witnesses appearing before the committee considering Bill C-204, that there were convenience stores-I believe the figure mentioned was twenty-where young teenagers could obtain tobacco. They were able to purchase tobacco in 19 out of 20 convenience stores, even young teenagers, even though it was illegal, so it is clear everyone is selling tobacco indiscriminately. That is why I think we should have stricter regulations to deal with this and with vending machine sales, which should be banned. There is nothing to that effect in the Bill before the House today.
We know there are many flaws in this legislation, though its purpose is a laudable and admirable one, which is to reduce tobacco consumption step by step. What we also knew, and we heard many comments in this respect. . . Madam Speaker, if you had seen the slides presented by the Canadian Medical Association! They were quite extraordinary for people like me who have never had a close look at the deadly effects smoking
November 23, 1987

can have. There was a lot of testimony to support the statement that cigarettes could be lethal, not just to those who smoke them but also to those who are exposed to ambient smoke.
Since the purpose of this legislation is to reduce consumption of a product that is bad for Canadians-I was a smoker once, I smoked for a long time before I gave it up-I think the purpose is admirable, and that is why we intend to support this Bill, but I think we will table a number of amendments to clarify the impact of the Mulroney-Reagan Agreement-the Canada U.S. Agreement. We intend to propose a number of amendments to clear up the problem about company names. We will also try to table amendments that will include what I consider to be our most important goal, which is to guarantee all Canadians the right to work in a smoke-free environment.
As I explained earlier, it is very odd that the federal Government has adopted regulations concerning federal employees, while, as we all know, Parliament remains sacrosanct, so that regulations that would prohibit federal employees from smoking as of 1989 would not apply to Parliament. This means that we, the Members of this House who will vote today on the second reading stage of this Bill and who will soon be voting on the third reading stage, that we are about to adopt regulations that would ban smoking by federal employees while we are not prepared to have the same regulations apply to our own employees.
So that is one more loophole in the regulations presented by the Minister with his colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski), a loophole that should be closed by amendments that will be proposed by the Liberal Party.
There are so many loopholes in the legislation that I think one could probably drive a Mack truck through them. In the course of discussions that will follow second reading of this legislation we will be introducing some amendments to it. We will try to improve the Bill. In particular, we will try to guarantee what we consider to be the primordial role of the federal Government, which is, at the very least, to protect working men and women who are exposed to second-hand smoke on a daily basis in the workplace.
We are not satisfied with the regulations the Government has introduced which deal with federal civil servants and which, in fact, exempt Parliament and thus our own employees. We are not satisfied with that approach. We will be introducing some amendments. On the whole we will come out with a better Bill.
For the Minister to achieve the objectives he is seeking, and I believe he is intent on achieving them, the Bill has to be strengthened. The Bill has to be more precise. The loopholes must be closed. Above all, the Bill has to protect people in the workplace. It cannot deal only with the issue of advertising. Unfortunately, Bill C-51 simply deals with the advertising
Tobacco Products
issue. A curb on advertising will assist in reducing consumption in a long-term strategy. It will not provide people with the protection in the short term that they need to be free from exposure to smoke in the workplace.
The study that the office of the Minister released today on second-hand smoke is damning enough evidence that Canadians should have the right to work in a smoke-free workplace, whether or not they happen to be federal government employees, working in Parliament or in the private sector on the federal or provincial scene. Those are the areas which we intend to explore in our further discussions on Bill C-51.

Madam Speaker, I congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) for finally bringing in Bill C-51 for debate today. It is an important step forward for protecting the health of Canadians. I am glad to see the strong stand that the Liberal critic for health has taken in her demand for a comprehensive approach to this question of the very serious numbers of deaths and diseases that are caused by tobacco smoking. The statistics are painful enough.
More than 35,000 Canadians who are smokers die every year from tobacco related diseases. Some 300 to 500 nonsmokers who are involuntary smokers die from tobacco-related diseases, for example, lung cancer and probably other diseases. A number of still births and perinatal defects occur as a result of tobacco-smoking on the part of the mother and, indeed, even from secondary smoke that affects the pregnant mother. These deaths are numbered in the hundreds. Fires are caused by the misuse of cigarettes. The deaths caused by fire are in the area of 200 to 400. This is indeed a very serious problem and I am happy to see this legislation before us today.
Bill C-51 would ban advertising of tobacco, cigarettes and sponsorships. However, there are a couple of loopholes. I also welcome the parts of the Bill that deal with labelling which are very important. They are a good step forward in dealing with this question and a matter not dealt with in my own Bill, Bill C-204. We are indeed breaking new ground.
I want to call to the attention of the Minister the need to plug a couple of loopholes with respect to advertising and sponsorship. The first loophole in the Bill is with respect to the point of sale advertising, for example, in local stores. This is where young children are purchasing their cigarettes. Local stores are bribed by the tobacco companies to have advertisements in their stores. Point of sale advertising must be completely banned and not left merely to regulation.
The other loophole is with respect to the partial ban on sponsorships. A brand name cannot be used but a company name can be used for sponsorships under this legislation. This is something which would not be permitted if Bill C-204 were enacted. It takes but a bit of imagination to consider that the tobacco companies could be incorporating new companies to make a company out of a brand name and thus escape the spirit and the letter of this law. We would like to see those

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
loopholes plugged. We know why the tobacco companies have to advertise. It is because some 35,000 Canadians a year are dying. They are smokers, the customers of these companies. Some 350,000 smokers, largely intelligent adult men, are quitting smoking. The tobacco companies have to replace their customers. They are doing this by looking for new markets. We know that they are going after children. That has been all too well documented. We also know that they are going after women. I am sorry to say that they have been enormously successful in their advertising directed at women. The women's movement is speaking up and talking back to the tobacco companies on that point. The symbols of emancipation are being used. Glamour, success and peer acceptance are being used to attract people to smoking.
One of the sneakier methods that has been attempted by a tobacco company to attract women smokers is worth citing here. I refer to a plan which, fortunately, has been scotched. Benson & Hedges wanted to put out a book on political women. My understanding is that this book would be sent to all the schools in Canada. It was a very clever idea. I was asked if I would give my permission to be included in this book. Other Hon. Members who are women were also asked to be included in the book. I am sorry to say that some of them fell for it. A woman member of the public was concerned about this matter and she sent a letter to the President of Benson & Hedges to protest. She wrote as follows:
I am very disturbed by your plan to publish a book on women in politics. I am convinced that this will have the effect of identifying successful women, women who are role models for other women-mainly younger women-with smoking, since 1 am well aware that the tobacco industry in North America has capitalized on the movement for women's liberation in an attempt to persuade feminists that smoking is the necessary corollary of success in the male-dominated world of politics, business and sport.
That was a very reasonable protest. In fact, it was very timely. Benson & Hedges replied to this public-spirited citizen in a letter which stated:
1 am in receipt of your letter-
First, let me say that I consider it rather presumptuous on your part to complain about something which is based, at best, on second or third hand information.
Inasmuch as you appear to have a Ph. D., I would have thought that irrespective of the discipline in which it was obtained, you would check your facts before committing yourself to paper.
Check the facts indeed. I have some of the facts here with me. One is a letter to myself inviting me to be one of these successful role models and to be included in a book on political women. The Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) was probably one of these women. Her name and face would go out to those young teenagers to encourage them.
We want to encourage young women to enter politics-of course we do. But do we want to sell them cigarettes at the same time? This is shameful. It is a good example of the tactics of this industry. It is going after young women in order to replace the intelligent older men who are quitting smoking. Fortunately, there was enough bad publicity on this matter
that the company apparently produced the book but did not distribute it.
Advertisers want to tell us that advertising of cigarettes does not work and that they are only interested in maintaining their brand name quota within the system. They have quoted some phoney statistics. They have tried to say in Norway, Finland and Singapore in full-page advertisements in newspapers this summer that ad bans in other countries have not been successful and that it would be counterproductive for us to go for an ad ban. The Canadian Cancer Society subsequently checked out all these so-called facts only to find that the situation was quite the opposite.
For example, in Norway, and the Minister has referred to this example, since the ban on advertising there has been a 15 per cent decline in the number of smokers. Yet exactly the opposite was claimed by the tobacco companies and the advertisers. It is very shameful that Canadians are being misled. They may not be too misled on this, because it is a little preposterous for the advertisers themselves. They have been coming to committee on my Bill C-204 and stating that advertising does not work, undermining their own industry. 1 think that advertising does work, and it should be part of the solution. We should have a counter-advertising program in order to encourage young people not to start, and to encourage those people who have already started to quit.
There has been a very dishonest use of so-called data. In the case of Norway, the clever trick was that it did not use ordinary tobacco made for roll-your-own cigarettes, and they included only one form of cigarette use which had gone up since the ban. But the total use had gone down. It also did not take into account the fact that there had been a population increase. It was not done per capita. So there was a very dishonest use of statistics in order to make their point.
The advertisers also tell us that it is not advertising that makes young people smoke, it is peer pressure. They actually did a study and asked children, "Are you influenced by advertising?" Human nature tell us that none of us likes to admit that we are influenced in a decision by advertising. We like to think that we made up our own mind. Quite naturally, most children stated that they had not been influenced by advertising, but some stated that they had been.
Even if it is a very small number, I suggest that one person dying from a tobacco related disease, from a habit that he or she would not otherwise have taken up, is too many. Thirty-five thousand Canadians die a year, and if only 5 per cent of those people started as a result of advertising, that is a sizable number. Even if it is only 1 per cent, that is 350 people. If it is 2 per cent, it is 700 people, and that is almost the murder toll in Canada. If anyone could find some brilliant way to reduce murder by 700 people a year, we would be very grateful to bring those numbers down.
November 23, 1987

Even if it is only 2 per cent and the advertisers are correct, and I do not think they are-but even if we accept their statistics, we should be pleased at the prospect that we could save 700 lives a year. I feel we will be able to save far more than 700. I feel there will be thousands and thousands saved, as this Bill and other measures undertaken begin to attack the consumption of tobacco.
We have been told by various people who oppose this Bill, and who oppose my Bill, that there are other measures that can be taken. Instead of legislation there should be a voluntary code. A voluntary code has been in operation for tobacco manufacturers. As the Minister himself pointed out, virtually every rule has been ignored and violated, time after time. I wish to cite a few concrete examples of how the tobacco industry violates its own code that is presently in operation. How could we have any confidence that they will reform and be different in the future?
The first rule states that there will be no cigarette or cigarette tobacco advertising on radio or television, nor will such media be used for the promotion of sponsorships of sports or other popular events. We all know that the tobacco companies buy advertising at sports events that are televised, so that their names and logos will appear. We know that they sponsor teams and require that their logos are on the sporting equipment and uniforms so that when the event is televised their name will get around, in this way getting around the fact that they cannot advertise directly on television. This is a very flagrant example of the abuse of their own code.
The second rule states that the industry will limit total cigarette and cigarette tobacco advertising, promotion and sponsorship expenditures for any year to 1971 levels, and that they will be increased only to compensate for cost increases or decreases-in short, the cost of living. Have they kept their word on this? We do not know exactly, because they will not release the data. I am a little suspicious on this one. If they had kept their word, why would they not release the data to prove it?
The sixth rule states that all advertising will be in conformity with the Canadian code of advertising standards as issued by the Advertising Standards Council. If this rule were obeyed, we would not have any advertising at all. The rule states that advertisements shall not display a disregard for public safety, or depict situations which might encourage inappropriate, unsafe, or dangerous practices. What could be more unsafe or dangerous than smoking itself? Thirty-five thousand Canadians are dying from it. This is far worse that any of the other types of activities.
I raised this at committee with advertisers. They stated that what they had in mind was boating accidents; we do not wish a boat shown in a billboard and not have the person wearing a life-jacket because that would encourage people to run out and get into a boat without a life-jacket and have a boating accident. These are the people who tell us that their advertisements for cigarettes never encourage anyone to smoke, but
Tobacco Products
somehow a boating commercial which showed someone doing something unsafe would suddenly encourage Canadians by the thousands to go out and have boating accidents. What nonsense.
The seventh rule states that cigarette or cigarette tobacco advertising will be addressed to adults 18 years of age or over, and will be directed solely to the increase of cigarette brand shares. I have never seen an advertisement that said, "We discourage you from smoking because it is very unhealthy, but if you are continuing to smoke anyway, try our brand". It does not happen that way. It is supposed to be addressed to adults 18 years or over.
It is very difficult to see a grocery or confectionery store without tobacco advertising that is located in an ordinary neighbourhood where there are families living and children going to those stores. There are bill boards all over. There are lots of bill boards on the Gardiner Expressway. They are lighted up and one cannot even read the health warning on those bill boards. They are all over the place. Canada's Wonderland has tobacco advertising. That is a place for children. Children thumb through magazines, although they may not be the subscribers, and they see tobacco advertisements there. The main drag in my riding, down Fourth Avenue, is a commercial street. Children use commercial streets. They go to stores. Fifty feet away from the street itself is a residential area. Yet there are massive bill boards advertising to children living in those neighbourhoods.
The eighth states that no advertising will state or imply that smoking the brand advertised promotes physical health, or that smoking a particular brand is better for health than smoking any other, or is essential to romance, prominent success, or personal advancement. This is the so-called "life-style" advertising. Tobacco advertisements are largely of this nature. Of course, there were the famous tropical fish advertisements that suggested that smoking is very good for tropical fish. Otherwise, they try to convince us that smoking is good for white water canoeing, kayaking, hang-gliding, exercising, dancing, and doing all those types of things. The example I just mentioned of Benson & Hedges wishing to associate cigarette smoking with successful woman in politics is absolutely contrary to their own code of advertising. It is a voluntary, useless code.
The thirteenth rule states that the warning will be prominently displayed. Of course, the warning on cigarette advertising is not prominently displayed. One can hardly read it, and it is a weak warning at that.
The tobacco manufacturers and advertisers tell us that we cannot ban advertising because it is a legal product. Advertising is limited for many legal products. Tobacco would not have been a legal product if we had had any idea of the harmful consequences when tobacco smoking began to become popular in Canada some years ago. It simply would not have happened. If we buy this argument, what it says is that once a mistake is made and a product becomes a legal product then you cannot

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
get rid of it. If it is a legal product or if it is an addictive product, it is not realistic to ban a product that is used by 6 million or 7 million Canadians.
Its use can be discouraged, and people who do not wish to smoke can be protected from being involuntary smokers. There are many things that can be done. The price can be raised to make it more difficult for kids to buy cigarettes. That should be done. Measures can be encouraged for farmers to get out of tobacco crops and to get into healthy, wholesome crops. That should be done. We should help farmers and their communities make the adjustments. There are many things that we can do. But to say that we cannot undo a mistake of the past is foolish, immoral, and there is no legal basis for doing that. We have a responsibility to act in respect to Canada's number one preventable health problem.
Another thing stated by the advertisers and tobacco companies is that if sports and arts sponsorships are banned, arts and sports will suffer. They make themselves out to be major contributors to this very important sector of national life. I want to spend a little time on this, because it is one of the more shameless misinformation campaigns we have seen. I want to deal particularly with sponsorship of the arts.
How much is it, for one thing? The companies would like us to believe that millions and millions of dollars are going into the arts, that they are the Canada council of the arts. Far from it; they are not remotely close to the CBC or the Canada Council in the amount of money they give to the arts. We are not even sure how much it is.
A couple of weeks ago, at a public meeting in Toronto, a representative of tobacco companies said that $20 million went to arts and sports. Nonsense, it is not $20 million. The Council on Business and the Arts indicated that it was $10 million to the arts alone. It is not $10 million to the arts alone. The full-page ads taken out by tobacco companies last summer indicated that $10 million went to culture and sports together.
Let us examine that $10 million figure. For one thing it is tax deductible money, and tobacco companies are paying tax at the rate of 35 per cent. Thus, 35 per cent of that money is our money. If it is $10 million, then $3.5 million of it is our tax money because we forgave it or reduced their tax bill. They are spending $3.5 million of our money.
How are they spending it in sports and the arts? Imperial Tobacco is the largest donor to the arts. It claims that for last year it spent $1.54 million on the arts. If we reduce that by the 35 per cent which was our money and not the company's, we are getting the sum down. If we look at how it is spent, the money goes down further. According to the Council on Business and the Arts, roughly half the money which goes to the arts is in the form of a gift, meaning that a ballet company can buy music, can pay choreographers, or can pay dancers. Half the money is not a gift at all; they do not even see the money. It goes for so-called services.
What are the services? They are not ballet slippers, music, or choreography. They are receptions at which the tobacco company's name is advertised. They are advertisements in newspapers of the ballet company with the logo of the tobacco company. It is a chance for the tobacco company to advertise its name without even the farce of that mild health warning. It is a chance to advertise cigarettes.
They have launched a campaign to convince people that they are spending a lot of money. I had a piece of work done through the Library of Parliament research services to try to find out exactly how much money they were spending on the arts or how much they were giving, and how much was involved in deals where they get advertising for it, in both cases tax deductible. So far these questions have not been answered. We are still awaiting precise information. However, it is very clear that it is not $20 million or $10 million. We are getting the numbers down in the case of the arts. It is well under $1 million for the arts. We are getting down to about $500,000 in contributions to the arts.
If they did not have this tax deduction, and if we did not allow this advertising and sponsorship, the Government would be collecting this money. It could be given to the Canada Council or to the arts directly or, in the case of sports, to sports organizations. That would be a far better use. I suggest very seriously that by permitting advertising and sponsorship in the arts and sports we are actually depriving these communities of better support. We should be giving them real money with which they can do what they want, instead of forcing them into providing services which effectively advertise tobacco companies far more than they help them in their own activities.
In order to convince people that tobacco companies are great patrons of the arts and promoters of sports, the companies undertook a massive campaign last summer. There were full-page ads everywhere at an estimated cost of $4 million, incidentally $4 million which was tax deductible. We are paying some of this money. We paid for more than $1 million of it. The irony is that taxpayers' money has been used more to try to convince Canadians that tobacco companies are promoters of arts and sports than in health promotion campaigns. That amount of money is more than the Minister of National Health and Welfare is paying for programs to discourage people from smoking. It is our money. Our taxpayers' money is being used to try to convince Canadians that we need arts and sports sponsorships when we surely do not need them and do not get value for our money.
I am pleased to see that the sports community is fighting back. I am pleased to see the leadership of athletes and of Physicians for a Smoke-free Canada, and the initiative taken by that group and others to have a smoke-free Olympics this year is a breakthrough. It is important and most desirable.
I was also very pleased to see that artists would not fall for this baloney on the part of tobacco companies, that they were the great patrons of the arts. Artists themselves, in cooperation with the Non-Smokers' Rights Association, have
November 23, 1987

taken out ads saying that they want a ban on advertising and sponsorship because they believe that children need a chance. They do not want to see children encouraged of to take up this dangerous product. I am glad to see that responsible attitude being taken by our friends in the arts and our friends in sports.
It has been suggested that if we ban this advertising it will only apply to Canada in that we get much of our advertising from the United States. It has also been suggested that Canadians will simply switch to the American brands advertised in American magazines. It is true, if the Americans do not ban that advertising this will happen in the case of magazine advertising. However, I suggest that there is no tobacco advertising on television or radio either in the States or in Canada, and that billboard advertising is only relevant for our country. Therefore the only area in which this is a problem is magazine advertising.
It so happens that roughly 60 per cent of tobacco advertising in magazines is of American cigarettes right now, but American cigarettes only account for about 1 per cent of the market. It is strange, is it not, that Canadians do not seem to want to smoke American cigarettes? We do not have any real reason to fear that there will be a massive switch to American cigarettes if we take the correct step and ban tobacco advertising and the Americans are slow.
Incidentally many Americans want their country to take this step as well. There are people in Congress who are working for ad bans. The United States is ahead of us in terms of a smoke-free workplace. They are ahead of us in some measures. Let us not give up on the Americans. Instead, let us lobby them to bring in parallel legislation which would be in the interests of all people who read magazines.
Members of the House have been subjected to quite a clever campaign on the part of the tobacco industry to convince them to vote against Bill C-51, and I guess indirectly against my Bill C-204. All Hon. Members will have received a large number of letters supposedly from constituents expressing their concerns-and perhaps Hon. Members have received some very genuine letters from constituents-which they should be aware were part of a strategy. It has been estimated that it cost $30 to get each letter to us.
What happened is that the public relations company managing the campaign sent out information to people it thought might respond. I am glad to say that only 10 per cent of them responded and that 90 per cent did not. They were given three follow-up telephone calls to encourage them to send in their letters.
1 will read a sample letter which was addressed to me: "You have succeeded in finding a symptom but have completely missed the issue". Then it talks about not wanting it to be illegal to advertise. These letters never mentioned health. They talked about freedom of speech. They were very high-minded about the Charter of Rights.
Tobacco Products
However, it is most interesting to look at the fine print. These are phoney letters, and people must understand that. How do we identify between a phoney letter and a genuine letter from a constituent? How do we distinguish the ones which came in from this campaign? They were all typewritten because the public relations company prepared the letters and the persons to which they were sent only had to sign them. There was no letterhead and they were not on their own stationery. Many of them were from small business people who have stationery. The same thing holds for the envelopes. They were matching envelopes, and different coloured stationery was used. It has the individual's name, the MP's name. It is Dear Mr. so and so or Dear Madam so and so. The letters are here but they are not on the letterhead of the company. Of course not. It was not the people in the company who wrote the letters, it was a public relations company that wrote letters to you, Hon. Members and to you, Madam Speaker. Hon. Members on both sides of the House have been flooded with phony letters purporting to be genuine letters of concern from constituents. Instead, this is a well heeled campaign on the part of the tobacco industry.
In case you are not sure about it, Madam Speaker, some of the letters are on white paper, some are on beige paper, some are on cream paper and some are on turquoise paper. None of them mention health, death, emphysema, heart disease, hospitalization or any of these assorted effects of tobacco use. Another hint that the letters are phony, beyond the fact that there is no letterhead, they are blocked to the left. Most Canadians when writing letters indent each paragraph. Some people do not, but it is very common. If you have 100 letters in your office with no letterhead, a matching envelope, the address typed out and blocked to the left, you can be very sure you have been a victim of a big hoax.
Some people who received these letters, that is your constituents and mine, have written back with little comments. They sent the letter back and signed it. One constituent says "I am completely opposed to this letter and urge you to support the ban on tobacco advertising". I am pleased to see that. I have another one from a constituent who has written across it "nonsense". The individual added a P.S. It says "Ms. McDonald, I support the banning of cigarette advertising even though I derive some benefit from it via my work in the theatre". Here is a public spirited person who can distinguish from his own benefit and the need to have controls. He also enclosed the letter he had received from the Canadian Tobacco Manufacturers Council, the perpetrator of this hoax.
The letter is to him and it says "In the postalgram we advised that you would receive a comprehensive information kit on this critical issue. You now have the kit in your hands. As you will note, it contains a letter and a stamped preaddressed envelope directed to your Member of Parliament. We urge you to sign and send the letter right away. Remember this damaging legislation could be passed into law soon.

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
Damaging, absolutely". It goes on and on in a tirade against the legislation.
But here we have a public spirited constituent who exposed this phoney hoax for what it is, as I am pleased to see a lot of people have done. Apparently 90 per cent of the people who were approached refused to go along with it. We should not be surprised about that, because we know that a strong majority of Canadians support a ban on advertising, and who support the other important measures which the House has considered and let us hope will continue to consider.
So much for the hoax and letters and envelopes. These are not genuine letters of concern from your constituents, Madam Speaker.
The measure before us now to ban advertising and sponsorship is important, but it has to be part of a comprehensive package. It alone will not really make a dent in tobacco smoking. We cannot have a proper education program for children so long as we allow advertising. Children do not believe the education program. They go into the classroom and the teacher tells them something about smoking, and then they go to the corner store to buy candy and there is a big cigarette ad. Children themselves say that if advertising is allowed, the Government must think it is all right. The fact that advertising is allowed says to people that it is not so serious that it should be banned. It is absolutely vital in order to have an education program that cigarette advertising be banned. That alone though will not do everything that we want to have done.
Recommendations have been made by many organizations. Let me cite one of the best, from the Non-Smokers' Rights Associations, list of measures that we ought to be considering as complementary to the ban on advertising and promotion. Amendments to Bill C-51 are recommended as follows. The Bill must terminate tobacco marketing to minors, a very large market of which we are aware. Features from Bill C-204 must be added to Bill C-51 to protect non-smokers from environmental tobacco smoke exposure in federally regulated workplaces and transportation. I will address a few words to that. Under existing Canadian tort law, tobacco manufacturers are required to give their customers detailed warnings with respect to the nature and extent of the risks. Some further points along that. There must be an immediate ban on spitting tobacco, so-called smokeless tobacco, an important measure that could be easily handled. It should be handled now before this habit becomes more prevalent and before we are in the same situation as we are with tobacco because it is hard to ban something that is widespread. The ban on the promotion of tobacco must include the industry practice of providing payments to retailers to feature tobacco products at the checkout counters.
That is why I think my Bill C-204 is a bit stronger in this respect. It is very clear that there should be no advertising whatsoever. It does not allow the loophole of point of sale advertising. We need measures at the workplace.
Treasury Board has by regulation introduced a number of measures, and we are pleased to see them. I look forward to the House of Commons, the Senate and the Library bringing in no smoking measures as well, but we do not have them yet, only partial measures.
Before a committee on Bill C-204, Labour Canada made it very clear that there would be exceptions to the no smoking rule. In places, for example, where federal employees share office space with the private sector, a provincial body, or somebody else, there would be no requirement for a smoke free workplace. Labour Canada did not know how many people would be exempted from the regulation but we suspect it is a very large number.
It is quite clear that the regulations the Government has introduced do not include the Armed Forces, the RCMP or Crown corporations. Several Ministers have said that they hope these other bodies will bring in regulations, but so far they have not. They have brought in only partial measures.
We need much clearer measures and full protection for the public as well as for employees. Regulation may not be adequate. We asked for legal opinions on that at committee. Is the Government sure that legislation will not be needed and that regulation will be adequate? We just do not know at this point.
It would be important in my view to meld Bill C-204 and C-51 so that we can deal with all of these aspects, the labelling which is contained only in Bill C-51, the smoke-free workplace, which is contained only in Bill C-204 and the advertising which is in both. We need to bring these measures together and come back with two Bills which cover the subject as adequately as possible. Let us hope the Minister will bring in other Bills and the related measures to which I have referred.

Addiction to smoking has taken epidemic proportions and we need a comprehensive program to fight it, to fight the mortality rate, to fight increasing tobacco use by youths, teenagers and even children. A total ban on sales to minors and children is what we need. We now have this legislation. Sanctions must be stricter, and this legislation which in practice has not been enforced must be effectively applied. Smokeless tobacco must be banned. We must have higher taxes as a means to discourage children, youngsters and teenagers from smoking. We need measures to encourage tobacco growers to switch to other health-promoting agricultural products. We must protect the workplace, we must protect the public.
Madam Speaker, we need a whole series of measures to fight smoking addiction in Canada.

I can see that it is one o'clock, Madam Speaker. 1 believe I have a couple of minutes left, presumably after Question Period.
November 23, 1987

subsubtopic: AWARDING OF CONTRACT TO BUILD FRIGATES-NEED FOR GOVERNMENT TO CONTROL COSTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Department of National Defence will soon award a contract for the last six of a twelve frigate construction program. Billions of dollars are at stake. Simple logic should prevail when awarding this
contract. The Department of National Defence should make sure that frigate construction expertise is developped in several locations of this great country. It should take advantage of the competition between two shipbuilding contractors in order to better control costs. Any monopoly situation would result in a price escalation much too costly to Canadian taxpayers.
The Department of National Defence should also question very seriously the representations made by the Saint John Shipbuilding Company to the effect that a frigate built outside of its own shipyards would cost an additional $79 million. That is sheer nonsense, Mr. Speaker, for the cost of a frigate expressed in 1985 dollars is $110 million. It is unthinkable that a responsible company should say this cost of $110 million would go up by $79 million as a result of a simple transfer from one shipyard to another.

subsubtopic: CFPR PRINCE RUPERT-PROTEST AGAINST BUDGET CUTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, residents of northwestern British Columbia are not amused by the Conservative-inspired proposal to slash the existing CBC station at Prince Rupert from 14 persons to 2. This station opened during World War II and has provided a vital cultural and information system to the far-flung coastal and internal communities for almost half of this century.
The slashing of CBC's operational and capital budget by $85 million has sent the corporation in search of ways to meet growing demands from Prince George, Kelowna, Kamloops, Vancouver and Victoria. No doubt these areas deserve more and better CBC service. However, where are those silent B.C. Conservative MPs when it comes to providing new funds to the CBC? They are silent, that is where they are. The Treasury Board has directed that CBC not enter into any extensions of service, including to British Columbia.
The CBC plan would slash $700,000 from CFPR. That is less than one-half the cost of the Stevens inquiry, a mere 1 per cent of the cost of the penitentiary in the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) riding and less than three days worth of interest on the $1 billion the Conservatives gave away to the Reichmann brothers on the oil deal.
The priorities of the Government are backward. It is time to push big business back from the trough. Taxpayers in the Northwest want service for the tax dollars they pay, and that means maintaining local CBC radio. Save CFPR!

November 23, 1987

subtopic: S. O. 21 DISASTERS EXPRESSION OF SYMPATHY TO FAMILIES OF VICTIMS OF FISHING VESSEL ACCIDENTS
S. O. 21 DISASTERS EXPRESSION OF SYMPATHY TO FAMILIES OF VICTIMS OF FISHING VESSEL ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my sincere condolences to the families and loved ones of the eight victims of the two tragic accidents which occurred at sea this weekend, one in the Magdalen Islands and one in Nova Scotia.

Saturday afternoon, in the Magdalene Islands, a thirty-one foot boat with five people on board was shipwrecked while crossing from Cap-aux-Meules to I'lle de l'Entree. All lives on board were lost.

In Nova Scotia, the vessel lost was from West Dover near Peggy's Cove. It was 27 feet long and had three occupants. It left port Saturday morning to check fishing nets set nearby. At 2 p.m. it was reported overdue and a search began. Winds were strong at the time. At 3 p.m. Sunday, November 22, wreckage was brought ashore and identified as being from the missing craft. The search is continuing under favourable weather conditions.
These tragic incidents serve as a grim reminder that the sea can be cruel and unforgiving. A recently released Coast Guard study into fishing vessel safety made 41 recommendations on improvements. These tragic incidents underline the need for fishermen and for all those who make use of small vessels to take the report and its recommendations very seriously and to ensure that their vessel operations are carried out in as safe a manner as possible.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN WATER POLICY-CALL FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members know, closed beaches because of pollution are a common experience for Canadians every summer. The causes of water pollution are known and we have the technology to take remedial action. We even know the cost-about $15 billion at last count. What is missing is the political will here in Ottawa to share the costs with the provinces and municipalities.
We had hoped to find an effective approach to sewage and water in the federal water policy just tabled. Instead, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) commits himself to more research and development. By substituting study for action he takes a page from President Reagan's acid rain policy book.
In contrast, we in the Liberal Party are committed to providing the federal share required to build sewer and water systems to protect our health and environment. If the Government is, as it claims, strapped for cash, instead of planning to spend billions of dollars on nuclear submarines it could provide such funds to ensure good drinking water for Canadians and prevent the closing of beaches every summer for many years to come.

subsubtopic: SLOWNESS IN APPLYING TECHNOLOGY-CHALLENGE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, "the future lies in knowledge-intensive industries and new technological applications .... We must compete with our brains, our ingenuity, and our creativity." These true words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) are reflected in the discussion paper entitled "Communications for the Twenty-first Century" recently published by the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald).
While pointing out that Canada has great strength in information technology and has, for 100 years, been a world leader in communications, the paper lays out the challenges of the future. These include database and software underdevelopment, slow technology application rates, and a need for expanded research. In addition, we have a fragmented and outdated regulatory system.
I recommend this excellent paper for ardent study by parliamentarians and all those with an interest in Canada's technological development.

subsubtopic: IMMIGRANT CHILDREN-NEED FOR SPECIALIZED TRAINING IN ENGLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, later today the House of Commons will be debating a motion to study literacy standards and targets for Canada. I wish to draw attention, therefore, to a crisis situation now developing in schools in our metropolitan areas.
In Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver, as well as other cities, many immigrants, both adults and young people, particularly refugee children, desperately require English as a second language if they are to have any chance in our society at all. Yet both the Toronto and North York school boards are reporting that they are being swamped by immigrant children
November 23, 1987

who require specialized training in English which they cannot provide because of a shortage of funds.
Yet these immigrants are entering Canada fully in compliance with Canadian law, and will pay Canadian taxes and make their contribution to Canada if they are given sufficient opportunity.
It does no good for the federal Government to say they are the responsibility of the provinces because education is a provincial responsibility, when the Department of Employment and Immigration and the Department of the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) have literacy programs to help other Canadians in their workplace and in their culture.
If the federal Government takes its responsibility for immigration seriously, it will assist immigrants and refugees to upgrade their language skills by helping in the funding so they will become Canadians in name and substance as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform the House that today marks the opening of College Week '87. The nation's colleges and technical institutes have again joined forces to launch their second annual Canada-wide public awareness campaign which goes through to November 29.

This week was organized by the Association of Canadian Community Colleges which, with its 125 affiliated members, is the only organization which makes it possible for colleges to agree on the major social, economic and cutural issues. Since it was established in 1972, through its constant co-ordinating efforts, the Association has helped Canadian colleges organize into a real network.

Canada's colleges and technical institutes are a national resource of the highest significance. The clear conclusion that emerged from the recent forum in Saskatoon is that all the key players in higher education, including federal and provincial Governments, must work closely together if we are to survive in a world of increasing competition. I know the colleges are fully prepared to do their share to meet the many challenges ahead.

subtopic: McGILL REDMEN WIN VANIER CUP-TRIBUTE TO UNDERDOG VICTORS
McGILL REDMEN WIN VANIER CUP-TRIBUTE TO UNDERDOG VICTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that this will not please you, nor will it please my Leader (Mr. Turner), but I would like to congratulate the McGill Redmen for their great victory on Saturday in winning the Vanier Cup, the national championship for Canadian university football.
This greatest victory in Vanier Cup history was against a UBC team which was undefeated in two years, and against heavy odds quoted against them. During the game McGill established nine records and their great fullback, Mike Soles, won the most valuable player award. He was not alone, Mr. Speaker. He was ably supported by their aggressive offensive line, the Crazy Dogs, and their outstanding defence, the Montcalm Maulers.
In a year when Montreal lost its professional football team we are particularly proud of this fighting McGill team. It is now evident that McGill is not only number one in academics but also number one in sport.

subsubtopic: FINAL CROP YEAR PAYMENT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement in Regina this past week by the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) was good news for western Canadian farmers who are suffering from low commodity prices and very tight quotas.
Over 85 per cent of Prairie grain farmers participate in the Western Grain Stabilization Program which they fund jointly with the federal Government. The 131,000 cheques will be in the mail by early December. This will bring the total payout for the 1986-87 crop year to $ 1.398 billion.
The Minister noted that on completion of the 1986-87 final payout the stabilization fund will show a $1.5 billion deficit. This means that all of the 1986-87 payout was made under provisions of the Act which allow the fund to borrow money from the federal Government.
The federal Government recognizes the value of the protection provided to grain and oilseeds producers under the Western Grain Stabilization Program and is currently considering amendments to the Act which would improve funding and make future operations even more beneficial to farmers.
November 23, 1987

subtopic: ACID RAIN-EFFECT ON NORTHERN SASKATCHEWAN LAKES
ACID RAIN-EFFECT ON NORTHERN SASKATCHEWAN LAKES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, lakes in the Canadian Shield in northern Saskatchewan and Alberta, like those in Ontario, are very susceptible to acid rain because of the composition of much of the rock around those lakes and the lack of buffering materials on the bottom of them.
The increase in the processing of tar sands in northern Alberta at Fort McMurray and the Cold Lake area has meant a considerable increase in the amount of acid rain and snow being deposited across the northern part of that province and northern Saskatchewan.
Professor Hammer of the University of Saskatchewan warned us in 1980 about the short and long-term effects of this increased activity. Monitoring has shown that some lakes are already below the accepted PH level.
The Governments of Canada, Alberta, and Saskatchewan must take note of the fragility of the northern ecology and ensure that air quality standards are rigidly enforced so that sulphur and nitrogen emissions will not continue to acidify and eventually kill our northern lakes.
The time for action is now, not after the environment has been made unsuitable for much of our fish population.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the NDP and the Liberals have a blurred vision of Canada, if indeed they have any vision at all. These negative individuals seem to think that Canada is an island, that we can live all by ourselves without trading partners and be happy ever after.
Well, I have news for them and the leaders of some of our unions who have the same blurred eyesight. Canada is not an island. Canada is a nation, and unless we have trading partners we will wither and die.
Under an NDP program we will share each other's poverty, but under the Tories we will share an expanding prosperity.
The Tory Party believes in Canada. We believe Canadians can compete successfully with the peoples of any other part of the world. We have confidence in our people. We are not afraid that the Americans will outplay us. Rather, we will
meet the challenges that free trade will open up to us and we will welcome the vast opportunities that will bring buoyancy and new jobs to our people.
The agreement for free trade with our American neighbours can be the catalyst that will give Canada its greatest period of prosperity ever. So on with free trade!

subsubtopic: NOVA SCOTIA-RICHMOND COUNTY DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-END OF FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision to terminate funding for the Richmond County Development Corporation by the Department of Employment and Immigration is a decision that is both irresponsible and grossly negligent. I cannot understand why a Government would be so insensitive to the needs of the communities in Richmond County which are desperately struggling to find viable business opportunities to enhance their own livelihood.
[DOT] (MI5)
It should be noted that community development corporations take a considerable period of time adjusting and educating the people whom they intend to serve. No community development organization is a great success on the first day. This is true of the Richmond County Development Corporation. Over the years it has been struggling to come afloat, and as of recent date it is doing extremely well.
From November 15, 1986, to August 15, 1987, the number of investments made by the Richmond County Development Corporation totalled 18, and the funds it has made available are approximately $327,700; owners' equity equals $553,000; and third party participation is over $1 million for a total project investment of $1,885 million.
I am appalled that the Government, which preached jobs, jobs, jobs in the last election, has treated this particular issue with such insensitivity.
What community development corporation will now want to go to Richmond County in order to assist individuals in that community after the way in which Richmond Community Development Corporation has been treated by the Government of Canada? The federal Government must change this regressive decision, because it is bad for the people who really count, the people of Richmond County in Nova Scotia.
November 23, 1987

subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES-HALIFAX HARBOUR PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Halifax today the Government of France is putting on a $1 million party for the Minister of National Defence and his entourage from Ottawa in an effort to sell a submarine. subtopic: CAPABILITY OF FRENCH SUBMARINE TO OPERATE IN ARCTIC
CAPABILITY OF FRENCH SUBMARINE TO OPERATE IN ARCTIC
speechtext:

I said lard sculpture, lard as in fat. In talking about being fat for the slaughter, this particular submarine being promoted by the French cannot even operate in ice.
What is the Government of Canada doing looking at a submarine that is not ice-strengthened, that cannot operate in the north and that is not even designed to use the very torpedoes for which we have already contracted? Has the Government's judgment been submerged in French largesse? We would be better off buying the lard model. At least then we could melt it down and have fish and chips while there are enough fish to fry.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the fish and chips are on the British submarine. The French submarine has Beaujolais nouveau.
Before either submarine would be purchased by the Canadian Armed Forces it would have to meet the specifications provided by the Canadian Armed Forces. They would both have to be modified to enable them to come up through Arctic ice and to operate in the Arctic environment. Both are within the technical capabilities of current design. The fact that those submarines that France now has and that are on display here are not designed for the Arctic is simply a result of the fact that France is not an Arctic power, and Canada is.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.
A couple of weeks ago in Halifax the Prime Minister acknowledged that one of the reasons for the Government's
unpopularity has been persistence in patronage appointees to a whole variety of government boards and institutions.
At that time the Prime Minister stated that Canadians wanted the Government to do better. In fact, he stated that they wanted him "to chuck the whole system out".
Considering that we now know that a substantial majority of the members of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency have direct connections with the Conservative Party, and that on the weekend it was confirmed that seven of the eight members of the Northern Ontario Development Agency have direct connections with the Conservative Party, and in fact the eighth is a known supporter and financial contributor, is this what the Government means by doing better?

Mr. Speaker, no. As my hon. friend knows, among other things we have almost doubled the number of women and ethnocultural representatives appointed to boards, commissions, and agencies of the Government of Canada. We have proceeded with high quality appointments of representatives of other political Parties and, I think, historic numbers of partisans of other political Parties to important jobs in the decision-making process of the Government of Canada.
But most of all we never suggested that political support ought necessarily to disqualify anyone from appointment. I hope that that is not the suggestion that my hon. friend is making. That is why we, under parliamentary reform, appointed or allowed the appointment of parliamentary committees to scrutinize very carefully, and allow parliamentarians to examine the credentials of people, be they NDP, Liberal or Conservative.
The parliamentary committee system is in place, and to my regret, I must tell the Hon. Leader of the NDP, that he and his colleagues have failed to use it. If they use it and examine political appointees under the GIC system, and if there is anyone who is disqualified for reasons of competence, we will be happy to bump him or her off the list. Until that time, the parliamentary system that is in place should be used to make sure that qualified Canadians can serve Canada.
Hear, hear!

Jean-Jacques Blais was appointed as a member of the Security Intelligence Review Committee. Harrison McCain was appointed as a director of Petro-

Oh, oh!

speechtext:

Many of these Canadians have been in business for many years but they do not have the resources to fight the Canadian Olympic Association in court. Can the Minister assure the House that the super sleuths of the COA will, in future, be less zealous in "going for the gold" in their attempts to protect Olympic symbols?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subsubtopic: END TO HARASSMENT OF SMALL BUSINESSES WITH OLYMPIC IN CORPORATE NAMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have discussed this very serious matter with Olympic authorities over the weekend and this morning. Although I understand the need for legitimate protection of trademarks, I made known to those officials in no uncertain terms the concerns the Government has in that regard.
I expressed and requested of the Olympic Trust on behalf of Olympic authorities that a more reasonable system be put in place and that they not be as over-zealous in areas where it is not likely there will be a conflict. I am happy to report to the House and to Canadians that I have received the following assurances today.
The Olympic Trust on behalf of Olympic authorities will be concerned only with those abuses that threaten legitimate conflict with Olympic and sport related matters, not small restaurants and tuck shops, and they will not be concerned
Oral Questions
with anyone using names or trademarks prior to 1980 unless it is in direct conflict with the Olympics. No further letters, threats or lawsuits will be issued without the personal approval of the president and the legal staff, something which has not been the case up until today.
As of today, Canadians from coast to coast can begin to prepare, as the Olympic torch travels across the country, to enjoy the most successful winter games in the history of the Olympic movement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock p.m. the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) had the floor. I recognize the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, earlier in my speech on Bill C-51 I exposed the hoax of the write-in campaign. The tobacco industry is spending more money to try to convince Members of Parliament and the Canadian public that they are great promoters of the arts than they actually give to the arts for artistic purposes. This is a terrific hoax and I urge Hon. Members not to be fooled by it.
In the time I have remaining I would like to refer to the economic consequences of this Bill. All kinds of scare tactics
Tobacco Products
have been raised in committee on my Bill, C-204, and generally about the economic consequences of this Bill. Let us understand clearly that when people quit smoking-and let us hope that many Canadians will quit smoking-they do not burn the money they thereby save. They spend that money on other goods and services such as entertainment, trips, food, clothes and movies. Other economic opportunities are developed by the change in taste.
The health concerns of Canadians do not mean that people will lose jobs. They mean that new jobs will be created in different industries. We should welcome this change. It would not, in any event, be justified to oppose a health measure to save the lives of in excess of 35,000 Canadians every year on the grounds that any number of jobs would be lost if we save these lives. Certainly we cannot trade dollars for lives. I hope no one would seriously suggest that. However, we do not even have to make that comparison or trade-off. There will be new jobs as people change their habits to new and, let us hope, healthier practices.
In conclusion, I very much welcome this debate on Bill C-51.1 fully support the matter going to committee. I can assure the Minister of the support of the New Democratic caucus, not only for this Bill but for a host of measures which will deal with the problem. We need a strong combination of Bills C-51 and C-204 which will deal with all the issues of advertising, sponsorship, labelling, and smoke-free workplaces and transportation. Let us make this good, strong health legislation for Canadians which we will be pleased to pass at third reading stage.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Stewart (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise as a very disappointed Conservative today due to this proposed legislation, Bill C-51. I hope that when it gets to committee and the Minister looks at it a little more closely there will be a change of heart.
I must say that I stand here as a biased person because in the real world my occupation is a wholesale distributor. In that distribution business some 68 per cent of sales are of tobacco products.
I would like to begin by giving a bit of background on this issue. It is not purely and simply a health question. We are really discussing a severe economic problem. Nearly 3,000 farm families in Ontario grow almost 90 per cent of Canada's tobacco crop. What will happen to them as a result of the Draconian measures in Bill C-51, and the worse measures in Bill C-204? Over 30,000 transient workers are employed in that industry, an additional 6,800 people work for the manufacturers, and thousands upon thousands of people work for the wholesalers and retailers.
The independent wholesale trade services some 50,000 small stores. I defy the Minister or anyone else to dispute that over 50 per cent of their sales are of tobacco and confectionery products. That is to say nothing of the advertising industry

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
which derives 20 per cent of its revenue from the advertising of tobacco, the purpose of which is nothing more than to switch brand loyalty. We have heard all kinds of talk about what advertising does to young people.
I have in my hand the Tobacco Advertising Bans and Consumption in 16 Countries with introduction and editing by Professor J. J. Boddewyn, Baruch College, City University of New York. This was done for the International Advertising Association in 1986 and its findings are in direct opposition to that which has been stated in this House.
Let us look at the growth in per capita cigarette consumption from 1970 to 1984 in some centrally planned economies. I do not think that there would be one word of advertising in these countries. In the U.S.S.R. there was an increase of 10 per cent, in Poland there was an increase of 14 per cent, and in Hungary there was an increase of 15 per cent. I could go on and on. However, the net increase in these countries was 16 per cent without any tobacco advertising.
More important, let us look at the annual compounded growth rate in per capita cigarette consumption since the introduction of advertising bans to 1984 in free-market economies. In Sweden there was a decrease of .7 per cent and in Norway there actually was a decrease of .5 per cent. In those countries they pay 75 per cent income tax and I do not think we want that in Canada. However, in Iceland there was an increase of .8 per cent, in Singapore there was an increase of .9 per cent, and in Finland there was an increase of 1.8 per cent. That is in direct opposition to figures which have been stated. In Thailand there was an increase of 3 per cent, in Italy there was an increase of 3 per cent, and in Taiwan there was an increase of 4 per cent.
Advertising is done strictly to change a pattern of brand loyalties. That is well documented in the industry.
Let us take a look at how hypocritical this is. The Government would like to have a market which buys the product and contributes over $4 billion in taxes to federal and provincial coffers, but does not smoke it. That is how hypocritical this whole thing is. The Government wants money but it does not want you to smoke.
Between January 1, 1980 and April 15, 1987 federal taxes increased 179 per cent. There is now 64 per cent taxation on a package of cigarettes. Ontario's taxes went up 200 per cent. The federal Government now gets 92 cents of tax from every $3 pack of 25 cigarettes. As I said, the total taxes received last year were over $4 billion.
With regard to the economic impact on the industry, in 1986 Canadians spent an estimated $6.4 billion on tobacco products. Wages and salaries in the industry totalled $267.7 million. Capital expenditures by manufacturers totalled $65.9 million. Property income taxes were $112.7 million, and transportation costs were $30.1 million.
The proposed Bill is almost a death blow to the tobacco industry. It is an insidious encroachment on freedom of
thought, belief, opinion, and expression, including freedom of the press and other media communications as guaranteed by the Charter of Rights. I did not think I would live to see the day that a Conservative Government would ever even suggest such a thing.
Statistics indicate that smoking has dropped in Canada since 1977 by 17 per cent among men and 10 per cent among women. That is not because of advertising or health reasons but because of over-taxation. Furthermore, it will continue. Within a few years we in the industry know that it will gradually disappear. However, it should never disappear as a result of removing the rights and freedoms of Canadians to make a free choice.
Any legal product for sale in this country should be free to be advertised. Canadians who are concerned about free speech should ask themselves what prompts the Government to infringe on fundamental freedoms when there are so many other solutions to the issue. Laws threatening our fundamental freedoms are unjust.
I am not suggesting that concern about smoking is not an important issue-far from it. We all realize that it is a concern, but laws must reflect tolerance and concern for justice and equity. Bill C-51 is inconsistent with these principles and Bill C-204 is worse.
Bill C-51 is also inconsistent with the Government's commitment to less government interference in our lives and is contrary to fair trade practices. In addition, it is censorship, and that is what happens in totalitarian states.
This Bill is the tip of the iceberg. What will be next, alcohol? Will we ban advertising on cars because they kill people? This is an insidious infringement on rights, and it is only the tip of the iceberg. It should be stopped now.
This legislation will affect farmers, manufacturers, retailers, advertising agencies, newspapers, magazines, outdoor advertisers and their employees. Sporting events, theatre and other artistic events sponsored by tobacco companies will be deprived of funds. For example, our Canadian Open will disappear.
Research and development will be curtailed because manufacturers will not be able to inform their consumers about improvements in product. The du Maurier clock will be gone from the shelves and the signs will be taken from the buildings. This is one of the most unjust measures I have seen.
A total ban on advertising will bring serious economic and social penalties, nothing else. People who wish to smoke will continue to do so and manufacturers will continue to produce tobacco products. I am willing to bet my next year's salary that 20 years from now there will be just as many people on the death rolls who were supposedly affected by tobacco smoking.
November 23, 1987

I want to read a couple of letters to give an idea of what the public really think. More than 50 per cent of people in the riding of Mississauga South, in answer to that Member's householder, said they were opposed to this Bill. The following letter to The Toronto Sun states:
I am a veteran who got into some heavy fighting in the western desert, particularly around Alamein and Tobruk. I don't need November 11 to remember those days or the buddies who didn't come home with me.
Yet on Remembrance Day I do stop and pay respect and remember why we were there, which was to fight for our country and our way of life-to protect the freedom of my generation and future generations.
However, this year I sat and thought not of my own buddies, but what we were fighting for and what they would think if they knew what was happening to the society they gave their lives for.
Most of the freedoms are slowly being taken away by minority groups that are always looking for one cause or another.
I am now retired, having worked hard for 50 years to make a good life for my five sons and a daughter How many freedoms they will have when they reach my age, I'm not sure. They are losing their freedom of choice with all these anti groups: Military, abortion, animal rights and many others.
This recent bill Toronto Council is trying to ram down our throats regarding smokers is going too far. Our ozone is slowly being destroyed by massive pollution. Our waters are being ruined by chemicals and toxic waste. We have thousands of tons of garbage we don't know what to do with and overworked and faulty sewage treatment plants. Diesel and gasoline fuels are spewed out daily downtown. Maybe they should spend as much time facing these major issues.
I consider myself a good citizen, a good provider and a good father. I am not a drunk, or a criminal. Yet I feel like a second-class citizen. Why? Because I smoke and will stop when and if I want to, not because a bunch of do-gooders think I should.
1 have another letter to my local paper, written by Diane Kwasniak of Scotland, Ontario. She states:
I would like to state my opinions on tobacco advertising and the tobacco issue.
There are two sides to every coin. Has it ever been proven that smoking causes cancer or any other illness? No, it has not.
Informed, fair-minded scientists admit that the mechanism of cancer is still unknown. Does Health and Welfare Canada agree with the findings of the International Cancer Conference? Information obtained concurred that over 90 per cent of smokers never develop lung cancer. As well, it was found by a consensus of scientists that a relationship between health and passive smoking cannot yet be determined. How can medical science be exact enough to state that 30,000 deaths each year are smoking-related? It is very obvious to me that scientific opinions differ on this question.
More importantly, one might ask why persons and institutions that the public expects to receive unbiased judgments from have so readily accepted such claims.
Radical groups have done their job well, both politically and through the media. In my opinion, 'the scare tactics' being used by these groups are ridiculous.
Has complete social change come about as suggested by Mr. Epp or is it being forced upon us? I think it is being forced upon us. The majority of Canadians are non-smokers. That does not mean that they do not accept what smokers claim, the right to choose to smoke with respect for others. Let us use good judgment and common sense in the tobacco issue.
What of tobacco farmers and related businesses who are being deliberately and gradually legislated out of business? All tobacco farmers have taken the direct impact of government legislation.
The pressures forced upon them have been devastating to many. Will they receive fair compensation for their losses?
Tobacco Products
Remember, tobacco is only one on a long list of suspected cancer-causing agents. Should it be singled out? Will red meat be next?
Now, the big question. Is tobacco a legal product or an illegal product? Tobacco is a legal product and therefore must be treated as such. Do we have the right to advertise legal product or do we not have the right to advertise a legal product? This is one of our basic rights. Let us not now be swayed by those claiming to be working for the good of us all.
Does our government realize that by banning tobacco advertising they are creating a dangerous precedent?
Radical groups claim this to be a 'major initiative', a first step. Is this what we, the people, actually want? I urge you to give careful thought to this issue. And, finally, I ask each of you, where do we draw the line on these issues and when do we take a stand? I say let it be now.
This Party stands for free trade and I fully support the concept of free trade. Canadians can compete with anybody. However, one cannot compete with all the international advertisers coming into this country through periodicals. Sixty-six per cent of the advertising in the tobacco industry in this country is for foreign products.
We do not see American cigarettes on the stands in the grocery stores of this nation, but Canadian cigarettes like Matinee, Export A and Rothman's. Those products are advertised well, and legally.
If cigarettes become the same price as a result of free trade we will see Marlboro country here. Cigarettes will continue to sell, regardless of the health issue. We will see the total destruction of a purely Canadian industry, aided and abetted by free trade. Do we want to destroy a Canadian industry? That is what will happen with this legislation.
The Fraser forum urges restraint. It discusses the hypocrisy of the taxation and the fact that the Government has no business acting paternalistically.
It goes on to make the same arguments that 1 have made.
A letter from the International Advertising Agency, which includes members from all over the world, states that this type of Draconian measure to prevent advertising does not happen in free countries.
It was pointed out in committee that 13 small outdoor advertisers will immediately go bankrupt if this legislation is put into effect.
In conclusion, I want to quote from Hansard of May 26, 1986, when the Minister said the following in response to a question by the Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald):
1 am saying to her very directly that if she is an expert in this field at all, and if she has looked at the effect that the banning of advertising has on reducing the number of smokers, then she will know that it is painfully few.
Those were the words of the Minister of Health on May 26, 1986, who said that the effect of a ban on advertising would be practically nil. He was right then. What made him change his mind in one year? I think it is those do-gooders about whom I spoke, a minority group, which exerted pressure without

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
looking at the economic realities of what we are about to do who caused this action to be taken.
The article by Stan Buda goes on to ask, "What has prompted him to produce a law that is an insidious encroachment of our freedom of thought, belief and opinion ... ?" He points out the fact, as 1 have pointed it out, that the number of smokers has dropped. His arguments are the same. He is a man in marketing who knows what this matter is all about.
