speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there questions or comments?

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member has just delivered a very forceful speech on this subject. Can he elaborate on what action he personally is intending to take if in fact the Minister does not share and see his view?

Madam Speaker, that is the simplest question in the world to answer, and I will not make any disparaging remarks. Obviously, the Government has a huge majority. Obviously, if this Bill comes in and is not changed, it will pass. There is nothing that I as one person can do about it. All I can do is to stand on my feet, as I have, to point out the idiocy in terms of economics as opposed to health that this Bill represents. The matter does not deal with just a health question. If it were just a simple question of health, I would not be standing here. What we will be faced with is the economic reality of what will happen in Canada if Bill C-204 and Bill C-51 are passed.
I am saying that this will have an effect not only from the advertising standpoint but from the standpoint of the manufacturer and the farmer. Why are we not out selling one of the greatest tobacco products in the world to China and other countries which sell a great deal of tobacco? Instead, we throw money at the problem. We pay farmers not to grow tobacco on land that is good for nothing else.
If the Bill comes back to the House and members of the committee decide in their wisdom that they will pass this craziness, then there is nothing more I can do about it. I will tell the Hon. Member one thing. I was not about to sit in my place and see an industry destroyed by a lot of do-gooders without trying to instil a little bit of sanity in those who support this measure.

Madam Speaker, I too listened to the passionate words of my colleague. Why does he label these individuals as do-gooders and categorize them as a small minority when he spoke about 7 million smokers as opposed to almost 20 million people who do not smoke? Why does the Hon. Member have to belittle those individuals when he is looking for respect for some of his views? I can understand some of the emotions he has expressed on the floor of the House of Commons since they
may rightly or wrongly express the sentiments of a great many Canadians. We will not move the debate ahead if we refer to a portion of Canadian society that objects to smoking for their legitimate reasons as do-gooders and a small minority when they happen to be very conscientious Canadians on the majority side of the issue.

Madam Speaker, if I left that impression perhaps I should not have. The do-gooder expression came from a letter written by a person who referred to these people as do-gooders. I do not think it is really relevant whether or not I agree with that point of view. I respect the position of those who are against smoking, of course. I respect the opinion of the 7 million who smoke. The Hon. Member must remember that the majority of non-smokers are not the ones making the noise. They are not. I am a non-smoker but I am very tolerant of the rights of smokers. But if any smoker does something that is obnoxious to the non-smoker, then I have no sympathy for that person. But Hon. Members will find that most smokers by and large respect the rights of non-smokers.
The fact that there are more people who do not smoke than those who do does not say that those people support this Bill, as my colleague who is sitting to my left will attest to in a moment.
I am not approaching this issue on the basis of medical grounds alone. The fact is that because there has been no proven cause of cancer does not mean that I would stand here saying that smoking is good for one. This is a matter of choice. Drinking is not good for one, nor is the overeating of any amount of sugar. Driving fast on the highway is not good for a person. The 10 per cent of medical doctors who take drugs know full well the repercussions are not doing something that is good for them. But it is their right if that is what they want to do.
When we start infringing on the rights of people in a place like this, then I must ask what we are here for. We are here to protect the rights of Canadians, not to take them away.

Madam Speaker, I have two short questions. The first is on the issue of the infringement of rights. Does the Hon. Member believe that we should be allowed to advertise, for example, sexual aids on television and in newspapers? I presume that his freedom of speech argument would allow carte blanche to the advertising of sexual aids and anything else.
My second question is this. Specifically, what steps has the Hon. Member taken, and I believe he has taken some constructive steps, with respect to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise)? For example, the Hon. Member said that the soil in the Simcoe area is not good for any other product but tobacco. I believe that there are alternate crops in the process of being developed. I am not prepared to write off Simcoe area soil as being useless for anything other than tobacco.
Could the Hon. Member enlighten us with respect to what steps he has taken concerning encouraging the Minister of
November 23, 1987

Agriculture to make cash payments specifically to farmers as well as cash payments in recognition of the financial losses that these farmers will incur as a result of this legislation?

Madam Speaker, tobacco farms are small acreage farms. The farms have a tremendous investment in them. We could not pay them enough money to make up for what their losses will be on those farms. The Elon. Member does not have to take my word for it. She can ask the tobacco farmers. She can ask the Minister. In committee we have been through this matter time and time again. If the truth were known, I think that the Minister does not support this measure. I think that anyway.
As far as tobacco itself and the acreages of farms are concerned, peanuts and other crops have been grown, but they do not work because the acreages are too small. I do not understand why we are not encouraging the export of our great Canadian tobacco and spending the money in that area instead of trying to pay off the tobacco farmer.
What about the thousands of workers in the manufacturing industry? Will they receive compensation? Will the small wholesaler receive compensation? What will be done for each small cornerstore at which a minimum of 50 per cent of their sales depend on tobacco? What will we do for them?
All we are talking about here is one small element of this matter, the farmer. I have read to Hon. Members the figures with respect to what this industry represents. This Bill involves the destruction of an industry. The Hon. Member had better have some amendments to fix this Bill up or else pull it for the good of Canada.

Madam Speaker, could the Hon. Member give us a quick review of the economic effects of the tax increases that have occurred over the last three years? My understanding is that the industry was very nearly devastated by those increased taxes which resulted in a reduction in usage and which created extreme cut-backs to the amount of acreage seeded. The number of people employed both on farms and in the processing and distribution industries were reduced. Did that not have a much more destructive effect than the potential slow decline in the industry that everyone seems to predict will happen with the inception of a ban on advertising? In fact, there have been some people who have concluded that there may in fact be an increase in the short term in consumption until four or five years from now when young people are no longer exposed to cigarette advertising. Only then, if at all, will consumption begin to decline.
Could the Hon. Member perhaps explain to us why he did not seem to be quite so concerned about what was a very great disruption in the tobacco industry caused by high taxation, as compared to the future outlook created by no advertising?

Yes, Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member has put his finger right on it. He is absolutely correct. It is the
Tobacco Products
increase in taxation that has made the tobacco market go down. Purely and simply those taxes have been raised, and smoking has gone down in Canada as much as 17 per cent over the last five years. Although acreage has gone down and there is a decrease in sales, the taxes have gone up. Those taxes have kept the government coffers full while destroying the industry, and that is absolutely true.
It is not the health matters, it is not advertising that has depressed the consumption of tobacco in Canada, it is purely and simply the price. The price is taxation. I absolutely agree with the Hon. Member.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Madam Speaker, I wish to declare my interest with respect to this Bill. I do not smoke. I have never smoked. I am allergic to tobacco, and I hate tobacco smoke. That is my interest, and I am putting it on the table right away.
I must say that I am not one of those virtuous persons who smoked for years and then gave it up. Today there are many people who did smoke and took the bull by the horns and stopped smoking. I congratulate those people. They have shown great wisdom and virtue. I am not one of those.
But I think that I have made it clear that 1 hate people blowing poison and dirt in my face. I think that I have the right to work and live in a smoke-free environment. Unfortunately, this Bill does not legislate a smoke-free work environment for companies and firms under federal jurisdiction. I would like to see a Bill that would do that. Unfortunately, this Bill does not. If I understood correctly, the Minister will attempt to encourage firms to put in measures which will result in a smoke-free environment, but it is not done by legislation in this Bill.
I respect those people who are addicted to smoking. Even though it is harmful to their health, I suppose that they have a right to smoke. But they have a right to smoke in their own rooms, houses, cars, backyards, and fields. I do not believe that they have a right to smoke in public places where individuals must go to work, or for other types of business or public affairs. They do not have a right to poison the atmosphere that some of us have to breathe when we earn our living.
To me it is simply a question of common courtesy, good manners, and of respect one for the other. If people wish to do something that is harmful to other people, they should do it apart somewhere, where it will not hurt those who do not smoke or do not like smoke. On that point, I must register my disappointment with this Bill. I support the Bill, but I am disappointed that it did not legislate a smoke-free work environment for firms under federal jurisdiction.
With respect to the ban on advertising in the Bill, I have questions in my mind whether this legislation will be successful. I suppose we have to start somewhere, and perhaps this is a start. But when we live in a country that is spread out along the United States border and we are overwhelmed with American magazines, publications, and newspapers which are

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
filled with tobacco and cigarette advertising, 1 have a feeling that although we ban advertising of tobacco products in Canada, the young people for whom we are concerned will still be subject to cigarette and tobacco promotions from across the border. When all is said and done, I am not sure how many, or if fewer people will be smoking.
In any event, people say that we have to start somewhere, and I suppose that Canada will be showing a good example by banning advertising. Hopefully, it will have some impact, but that remains to be seen. In my opinion, more progress could have been taken on this important subject more directly than in this manner.
For all of those reasons, Madam Speaker, I believe that this Bill requires much examination in committee. We are prepared to vote in favour of it as soon as possible and have it sent to committee where witnesses representing the different interests can appear and put on the record the facts with respect to health, economics, the agricultural side, be cross-examined and questioned by Members of Parliament, and then perhaps there will be amendments to the Bill. If the Bill is lacking in some respect in dealing with the evil of smoking, perhaps it can be strengthened in order that we end up with less smoking and damage to our health than we have at the present time.
I simply wished to intervene to make clear my position with respect to those things. For years I could never understand how people who would object and be upset if, for example, I dumped all my snow on their walk, but they would sit in a car with me and blow their cigarette smoke in my face. For years there has been a double standard.
I was listening to my hon. friend across the way when he almost suggested, and I do not know if he meant to do so, that to smoke and to promote cigarette smoking was a basic right. We have the right to drive automobiles, but we are not allowed to drive on any side of the street. We are not allowed to endanger the rights or the health of other people. Under certain circumstances, we are allowed to use firearms-too much, in my opinion-but not in a manner that is harmful to other people. We are allowed to do a good many things, but not in a manner that is harmful to other people. Until recently, that has not been so with cigarettes. Until recently, one could enter a committee room in this Parliament and sometimes the chairman could hardly been seen for the smoke that was in the air.
Things are changing. The message is getting through to some people that this is killing them in large numbers; it is distasteful, uncomfortable, and nauseating. Let us pass this Bill, send it to committee, and come out with a better Bill.

Mir. Don Boudria (Glengarry-Prescott-Russell): Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this afternoon to speak on second reading of Bill C-51, a Bill the House has been waiting for a long time. The Bill had its first reading quite some time
ago. In fact, I have here a press release dated April 22, 1987, in which the Minister announced that he intended to table this Bill in the House of Commons.
Madam Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to prohibit the advertising of tobacco products. It also proposes to prohibit the use of brand names in advertising by sponsors of events involving sports, cultural or other activities, except in cases where the name of the company and the name of the tobacco product are identical.
In my opinion, we have here an element of unfairness because, for instance, a company whose name happens to be the same as that of its tobacco product will have an advantage over other companies, such as Imasco or Imperial Tobacco which have no products or merchandise bearing their names, and so some companies will have an advantage over others.
I have a problem with this particular point, and I hope that in committee, Government Members and, in fact, Members on both sides of the House will find a mechanism to make this part of the Bill more equitable than it is now.
Another point was raised by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), namely that tobacco products advertised in American magazines would be coming into the country anyway, so that we would still have tobacco advertising.
I don't know what steps the Government intends to take to ensure this doesn't happen, because after all, Madam Speaker, if it is bad for Canadians to read Canadian advertising that encourages smoking, I believe it would be just as bad for Canadians to read American brochures or magazines containing similar information.
I hope the Government will find a way, such as income tax deductions for advertising placed outside the country or something like that, to discourage Canadian businesses from inserting this kind of advertising in American magazines, when they will no longer be allowed to do so in Canada.
If nothing is done about this, the Canadian periodicals industry will suffer as the U.S. takes up the slack and I think there is a way to strike a balance so that everyone is treated fairly.
This Bill will also prohibit the use of premiums, Madam Speaker, and it's about time. Imagine that tobacco manufacturing companies, cigarette manufaturers mainly, were giving away-I don't know if they are still doing it but they used to- small coupons which people can collect and which entitle them later to order almost anything, such as an electric kettle or whatever-I think as part of a scheme to encourage people to continue smoking. They even offered gifts which appealed to young people. For instance, when a company offered something like a bicycle, if that was not a scheme to encourage young people to smoke, I wonder what it was. I am pleased, therefore, to see this practice banned.
November 23, 1987

In my opinion, most Canadians, whether they are for or against Bill C-51, are at least in favour of eliminating this sort of premiums.
As most of Hon. Members, Madam Speaker, I received a great many letters on this issue. I have even brought some of them with me here. Many of these letters sent to Members of the House indicate their opposition to Bill C-51.
Madam Speaker, I find it rather strange that all these letters look alike. They were not only similar in appearance, but identical. We could therefore assume that they might have been prepared by some people for the signature of others, and I wonder if these people are not those involved in the tobacco industry through their travelling salesmen who go and sell in all convenience stores and commercial establishments in the various electoral ridings in Canada.
The constituency which I represent has some 42 different communities. I find it more than passing strange that the letters of protest against Bill C-51 were relatively similar if not exactly the same. They were sent by store owners in every part of my constituency. I am led to conclude that such was done in co-operation and at the urging of tobacco industry representatives.
What we are discussing today is not whether or not tobacco farmers, particularly those in Ontario, have a right to survive or a right to continue production. Of course I understand that there is also tobacco production in the Province of Quebec, in an area with which the present occupant of the chair is quite familiar. Obviously tobacco farmers have a right to continue to have profitable farming establishments and to survive. Of course we all want that as Members of the House, but let me indicate that our efforts must be directed in such a way as to find alternate crops for tobacco farmers and to find sufficient financial means to assist those same farming entities in producing something else.
I know it has been stated by others before, but let me ask this, what would be the reaction if someone were to walk into the Chamber today and present the following proposition to us as parliamentarians-they have a great new idea which will produce a product that causes cancer of the lungs and an assortment of other diseases, that creates smoke all over the place and a horrible smell, that ruins clothing and everything else, that pollutes the environment and wastes many resources, and that generally results in considerable health care costs for people who would suffer as a result of consuming the product? Would we accept the marketing of a product with those characteristics?
1 think we already know the answer to that question. If someone wanted to introduce such a product, we as parliamentarians would not accept it. Society as a whole would want us to reject a product with those characteristics.
Tobacco Products
However, it was a number of years ago that tobacco was discovered and, unfortunately, marketed. It is now widely available. We are not discussing whether or not we can place the product on the market. As I said, that is an unfortunate reality, and I say that as a reformed smoker, one who partook in the weed some years ago but gave it up in approximately 1970.
How young were you when you started?

Since then I have perhaps smoked once or twice in the mid-1970s. I hear a member of the New Democratic Party asking me just how young I was when I started smoking. I thank the Hon. Member for that inherent compliment, and I accept it.
You owe me one.

The Hon. Member is quite correct. I owe him one for that generous remark which indicated how young I still am.
However, that being said, I want to indicate to the House that I support the Bill. I would like it to proceed. I hope that it gets full and thorough consideration at committee, complete with the contributions of parties on both sides of the issue. I hope we will hear from people in the advertising industry and anyone who may be adversely affected. Notwithstanding that, I want to indicate that my purpose in requesting the input of the tobacco industry, the advertising industry and so on is not to change the mind of this House nor its Members as to the benefits of having the legislation, but rather to ensure that the legislation is fair when it is passed. In so doing, not only will it be more equitable but the law will be more beneficial to all Canadians when applied in a just and fair manner.
The tobacco industry started this and assisted many people in this campaign to defeat Bill C-51, an exercise in futility on its part but one on which it spent considerable dollars. The irony is that the dollars spent are, in large measure, tax deductible because they are seen by the authorities as being a legitimate business expense. On the other hand, volunteer organizations have been fighting this Bill with little or no resources of their own other than small contributions which they have received from individual Canadians.
It is sad when indirectly the taxpayers dollars can be used to promote a campaign which is ultimately to the detriment of the lives and health of many Canadians. However, that is another matter which we can discuss at the time we review the Estimates of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) or in some other format, but I wanted to raise that concern of the deductibility of expenses as it pertains to the promotion of a campaign against Bill C-51.
A parallel campaign was started by some groups in Canada in response to one started by the tobacco industry. I want to

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
congratulate those people, particularly the volunteers who worked very hard in starting that parallel campaign, particularly those affiliated with the Canadian Cancer Society. Last Thursday I received a letter in my office signed by Mr. David Hill of the Canadian Cancer Society in which he informed me that 135 of my constituents died last year as a result of tobacco smoking. That was a statistic which I did not know about before. We all know about the evils of tobacco. But let me tell you, Madam Speaker, more than anything else, hearing that 135 of my constituents had died was enough to convince me, had I not been convinced already, that we must do everything within our power to cut down on the use of tobacco.
There are deficiencies in the Bill. We all know what they are. Others have recited them today. Federally regulated agencies and corporations will not be subject to the smoke free environment provisions even though the federal Government itself is. I am told that Parliament is not bound by the Bill. We should be an example as an institution to other agencies whether or not they are federally regulated in providing within Parliament itself a means to ensure that there is on Parliament Hill a smoke-free environment.
Members of the House will know that I supported the initiative placed before us some time ago by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) who brought forth a private Member's Bill on curtailing the use of tobacco in the federally regulated workplace. I want to take this opportunity to congratulate the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood for the fervour and zeal with which she defends the point of view in which she strongly believes. I am not sure that I would always have the kind of fortitude that she has when speaking on the issue and when insisting on having a smoke-free environment in groups and meetings, but I admire her for that. I wish her every success with her own Private Members' Bill.
I do not want to delay this process unduly in the House today. I want to end simply by reminding Canadians that some 35,000 people die every year from the effects of tobacco smoking. It is high time that we as a society came to grips with that. I will not even mention the millions and millions of dollars wasted in health care for a totally preventable disease nor the human suffering and so on that is associated with it.
We should adopt this Bill, perhaps with modifications and improvements at the committee stage. But we must spend more money on educating the Canadian public. One aspect particularly alarms me. Young people have vast knowledge on the evils of smoking, but a large number of them still smoke. Let me mention young women who smoke. Why do I single out young women? It seems to me that the relative percentages of young women smoking are increasing while in every other group those percentages are decreasing proportionately. Given that we know of the effects of smoking on women of childbearing age as well as all the other facts we have spoken about today, there is a definite concern in that regard. I hope the young women of Canada will seize the opportunity of availing themselves of better information, learning of those evil side
effects and hopefully will "butt out", as the expression is, as soon as possible.
It is my hope that there will be a parallel campaign by our Government to discourage young people from smoking. That can only be done with a proper educational program. Hopefully the federal Government can work together with the provinces in order to provide material to schools and provide statistics, some of them gruesome, for instance, that 135 of my constituents died from the effects of smoking, that 35,000 Canadians die every year. What about the countless numbers who are sick as a result? Our young people will be better informed so they at least will not make the same mistakes as others have before them.
[ Translation]
Having said that, Madam Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity to take part in this debate this afternoon, and I dare hope that without further delay the Parliamentary Committee will make the necessary improvements to this Bill and that the House will pass it shortly, since if is long overdue.

Madam Speaker, what is the Hon. Member's feeling about alcohol? Would he prohibit advertisements of alcohol as well? I understand alcohol is much more dangerous than tobacco. It kills many people and creates many social problems. Would he ban advertisements of alcohol?

Madam Speaker, that is an interesting question. There is no such legislation before the House at the present time. However, if the Member's Government wants to propose such legislation, I will be willing to deal with it and give that my support as well in terms of advertising alcoholic beverages. The Member will know that there are certain restrictions on that right now. I do not know if some of those restrictions are still there, but for instance, there are provisions prohibiting lifestyle advertising. In other words, companies cannot promote the sale of alcoholic beverages by portraying a fast-lane lifestyle, something that had been depicted upon occasion. Alcoholic beverage companies, particularly beer manufacturers, were told to cut that out. There is still too much of it going on, however. The "Spuds MacKenzie, real party animal" advertisements are the kind of advertisements that I find totally disgusting.
The evils and side effects of alcoholism are also very serious, things with which we as a society must contend. Many other things are very serious as well, as some Hon. Members have mentioned. It is not simply a question of, since we are now banning tobacco advertising, should we not ban something else at the same time. That is not the question before us. The question before us is a very serious one and it deals with curtailing the use of tobacco by means of discouraging certain forms of advertising.
November 23, 1987

Some prohibitions like this already exist in the area of liquor advertising, but this particular legislation will go even further. Later, if the Government wishes to do so, perhaps we could deal with the same provisions for alcohol. There are differences though because the constitutional authority for the advertising and distribution of alcohol, depending on where it is, does not always lie at the federal government level, as the Hon. Member will probably know.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 66, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The Hon. Member for London-Middlesex (Mr. Clifford)-Via Rail-Service in Windsor-London-Toronto-corridor; the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald)-Trade-Film distribution industry-Film import licensing/Book publishing industry; the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet)-Trade-Canada-United States trade agreement-Marine transportation industry/Delay alleged in proceeding with legislation/Request that Minister not sign transportation annex to agreement.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Epp (Provencher) that Bill C-51, an Act to prohibit the advertising and promotion and respecting the labelling and monitoring of tobacco products, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Madam Speaker, I am a very strong believer in a Member representing the wishes of the majority of his or her constituents to the greatest possible degree. Throughout my legislative life, I have followed that principle.
I cannot follow the thinking of Hon. Members who think that once they are elected, they have more brains than they had before and they suddenly have the ability to tell the people what is good for them. I do not follow that thinking at all.
I was most disturbed when, during a vote taken in the House a few weeks ago, so many Members said that although their constituents wanted them to support the reinstatement of capital punishment, they did not agree. In my view, that is not
Tobacco Products
democratic. Our democracy has been set up in such a way that the Member represents to the greatest possible degree the thinking of the people who sent him or her here. Whether or not I agree with the thinking of my constituents is a matter on which I have to satisfy myself.
If I have taken a definite stand against a certain issue before an election, I do not think my constituents have the right to ask me to go against that view because I was elected on that particular premise. For instance, I am strongly opposed to abortion. Every year in Canada, 50,000 babies are murdered in the womb, and I oppose that. I do not think it is right and I do not think it is moral. When 1 stood for election, I made it very clear to my people that if elected, I would endeavour to prevent the abortion of human babies, human beings. People who would now ask me to vote in favour of abortion do not have the right to do so because I was elected with their knowledge that I would not support abortion.
I also made it very well known that I would work toward the reinstatement of capital punishment, the execution of those who deliberately plan and kill other human beings. If people ask me to support the abolition of capital punishment, I cannot do so. That is the premise upon which I was elected and that is what I believe.
If I have not made clear to my people my stand on certain items, then 1 believe it is my duty to represent the thinking of the people who sent me here to the greatest possible degree. That is the policy I will follow in connection with this Bill, even though there are many aspects of it with which I do not agree.
Of all the letters I have received on this Bill, probably three to one are in favour of it. What about the minority? I think their rights should be outlined, but I do not think that I should support the minority as long as the majority of my people want me to support the Bill. Therefore, I would like to deal with the principle of the Bill in that context.
First, Bill C-51 does not stop people from smoking. I believe we must make that clear. Those who argue that people should not smoke should realize that this Bill does not provide for that. The Bill does not stop anyone from smoking nor does it stop anyone from growing tobacco.
What does the Bill do? The Bill prohibits the advertising and promotion of tobacco products. That is the first part of the Bill but I think we must stop there and look at that.
Are we to prohibit the advertising of everything that Members of this House or members of the Government do not like? Let us look at the statistics we have heard. I accept the statistics given by the Minister and other Hon. Members because I have no way to prove otherwise. However, when they tell me that so many thousand people have died from smoking, the immediate thought that comes to my mind is, what did those people do with the rest of their time? Did they drink, did they carouse, did they stay up all hours of the night? Did they

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
dance from late at night until early morning? Did they drink wine to excess, did they eat to excess?
One lady in my constituency said to me one day: "I hear you are going to stop me from smoking". I said, "No, the Government will not stop you from smoking. The Bill says that there should be no advertising of it". She said: "Everything I like is either fattening, immoral or illegal". 1 said "Well, that is too bad. You must like the wrong things".
She said "I like Boston cream pie. Is that wrong?" I said "No, but if you eat Boston cream pie four or five times a day, that is wrong, but that is up to you to decide. If you want to ruin your body with sugar, fats and sweets, that is your business".
She said: "I like banana splits". Well, I like banana splits too but I do not eat them very often. I eat them perhaps once a month or once every five months because I have to make the House of Commons hockey team and I would never make it if I had banana splits every day.
How many of those people who died from smoking used drugs? 1 find it amazing when I hear all the talk against tobacco and then find that those who talk against tobacco-1 am not talking about Members of the House, I do not know whether or not they use drugs although 1 hope not-are great marijuana supporters or supporters of drugs that are even heavier and worse than marijuana.
How many of those who died from smoking did heavy work? Some of the coal miners in my constituency who smoked died because they were so anxious to be the top loaders in their mines that they worked in the smoke. They loaded coal in the smoke and they got smoke in their lungs. They got what is called in the mining industry black lung, and many of them died from black lung. They got it not because they smoke, but because they worked in the smoke created by the dynamite used in the mine.
I wish those who produce these statistics would tell me something about the other habits of the people who died from smoking. I accept the figures, but I cannot help but wonder if they also drank to excess. Did they overeat? Did they use drugs? Did they carouse to all hours of the day and night? These things have an effect on health, too.
I do not think we want to argue the point that smoking is good for you. I would not argue that for anyone, anywhere. I do not think it is. However, 1 have no right to say to my neighbour or friend or the person sitting beside me in an airplane that they have no right to smoke. If they want to smoke, fine. Many people say that people have died because of other people smoking. I take that with a grain of salt. I have been a non-smoker all my life. As I said before, I smoked only one cigarette in my life. That was the same day I kissed a girl for the first time. I never smoked a cigarette after that.
I have lived with smoking. I have been in rooms in schools where three-quarters of the teachers, particularly the women, were smoking. A Member said that more women smoke than men. I went to a drama school in Banff one year, the Banff School of Fine Arts, and out of 30 men and about 60 women, five men smoked and 45 women. As we sat in the room the atmosphere was sometimes full of smoke. I have attended legislative committees, provincially more so than federally, where three-quarters of the people were smoking. I have not died yet from that second-hand smoke. I may not like it, but I do not think it is killing me. It might if I caroused all night or drank or some of these other things too much. It could have an effect. However, I think we over-emphasize second-hand smoke.
The Bill prohibits advertising. It does not say you cannot smoke. I want to say on the record that I strongly support that part of the Bill which deals with labelling. I think every possible opportunity should be taken to let people know what smoking will do to them. Even though Churchill lived to be over 80 and smoked a cigar almost continuously, I do not think we can say that smoking cigars is good for you. I heard one man say his grandfather died from smoking at the age of 96. I do not think we can draw conclusions from that type of example.
We have a responsibility, particularly to the young, to tell people that smoking is dangerous. It is not good for them. They will not be the best athlete they could be. They will not be the best person they can be if they smoke. I am not going to say it is going to affect their brain or they will not do well in school. Many of our scientists and geniuses are smokers. We have to recognize that smoking is one item and only one item affecting a person's health.
I support every possible way of labelling tobacco products to indicate what the danger is. That is the program followed by the U.S. Whenever anyone takes out a cigarette, they see on the package, not in little tiny letters but in large letters, what it might do to their health. I support that because I think it is excellent.
The Bill also deals with monitoring. I do not know just how we are going to monitor this. When I look up the meaning of the word in the dictionary one reference is that it is supposed to give you a warning of the approach of crocodiles. I do not know whether or not that has anything to do with smoking, but I do not know exactly how the monitoring is going to take place. If it means going into our schools and telling boys and girls of the danger to health from excessive smoking, then I am all for it.
I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has a responsibility to keep people healthy. I would be most disappointed if our excellent Minister did not take a stand against smoking just as he takes a stand against drinking, certainly excessive drinking, or excessive eating, or excessive carousing. I have not heard him speak of those things, but I know he lives a very exemplary life and I
November 23, 1987

appreciate that very much. He has a duty to make sure that this legislation tries to keep people healthy.
When we come down to it, I would like to see smoking curtailed. I have never opposed increasing taxes on tobacco products for that very reason. It has had the effect of making many people quit smoking. A young man said to me just a few weeks ago that he smoked until the price became so excessive that he just gave it up. He made himself give it up because he could not afford it. It was not fair to his wife or young child, so he gave it up. That is one way of doing it. However, prohibiting advertising sticks in my gullet. That bothers me. There are so many other factors that lead to death, so many other things that are not good for your health, which we do not prohibit from being advertised.
I think advertising is somewhat of a right. It is not a total right. I remember that in the provincial legislature a few years ago I made a statement that it was wrong for the tobacco companies to show an athlete being cheered by the crowd and then lighting up a cigarette. What stood out most conspicuously was his smoking the cigarette. In the same way I opposed the kind of advertising that shows a great pilot of an aircraft getting off the plane and drinking a glass of beer or whiskey. That is not what made him great. That is wrong advertising.
I do not take a stand for total abolition of advertising. Some advertising is okay. I cannot see anything wrong with a grocery store saying it sells cigarettes and cigars. That is not going to make anyone go in and buy, and I cannot see anything wrong with it. That is part of business. In the same way I do not like people to say you have to advertise in one language. I do not agree with that. Advertising can be in any language that the vendor wants to use if it is legal in that country. I have no objection to people in my constituency advertising in Ukrainian, Russian or Lebanese. That is their right. However, this other type of advertising is questionable because it tries to make people think that you become great because you smoke or drink. That is wrong.
I congratulate the Minister if that is what he has in mind. However, I hope we do not go to the extent of telling small stores that they cannot advertise cigarettes. There are so many other things which are wrong which are allowed to be sold in grocery stores, drug stores, and cornerstores.
We are at second reading stage on this Bill. We are dealing with it in principle, and this is the time to say what we think is right and what we think is wrong with it. From here it will go to a committee. I hope that the committee gives careful thought to everything that is said during this debate. The members of that committee have the authority to change anything in this Bill that they think is not right. I believe that there are some aspects of the advertising of tobacco products that should be corrected.
I believe in the parliamentary system. We can speak for or against legislation and make suggestions. A committee of our
Tobacco Products
peers will decide what is best for Canadians as a whole, what is most in the interests of a healthy and virile Canadian people.
I look forward to having the members of that committee deal with this subject in light of all the facts so that we can be fair to those who smoke as well as to those who do not smoke and so that we do not take away rights which people of this country properly enjoy.
We have prohibited advertising in part many times and that is fine. We should prohibit advertising which makes a hero of those who smoke or drink. However, let us not try to stop the little storekeeper from saying that he sells cigarettes.

Madam Speaker, I listened attentively to the remarks of the Hon. Member. He indicated that he is in favour of labelling tobacco products with information on the ill effects of smoking. I agree with him on that point.
The Member indicated that a number of people have smoked and lived to a ripe old age. He referred to Sir Winston Churchill and another gentleman who was in his 90s when he died after having smoked for many years. We can, of course, easily remember people who live for a very long time. However, using the same logic, we would not remember very well those who died at the age of 40 of the effects of tobacco smoking. There are many people who would have had brilliant careers and whom we would have remembered had they not died prematurely as a result of smoking.
The Member says that he is against lifestyle advertising, which is one expression to describe it. He says that smoking should not be associated with an athlete or other such person. In that same vein, I am quite upset with certain lifestyle advertising which pertains to young women. We do not often see advertisements for cigarettes featuring someone with a bloated face and red eyes who is 150 pounds overweight. Young women in advertisements are always very slim and shapely. This contributes to a belief by some people that smoking helps to keep you slim. There is, therefore, a reluctance by young women to kick the smoking habit based on the erroneous, in my view, belief that it contributes to a more slender figure.
That has nothing to do with athletics or any such thing, but I consider that kind of advertising as offensive as that to which the Hon. Member has referred. The message in that advertising may be even more insidious because it is not up front but it is there. 1 am sure that the people involved in tobacco advertising are aiming their product at that market. It has obviously crossed their minds that some people would refrain from kicking the habit based on the hypothesis which I just brought forward.
The Member said that an advertisement in front of a store indicating that the store sells cigarettes does not make people buy a product. If it does not make people buy a product, what is its purpose? That is obviously a rhetorical question. We all know that the purpose of advertising is to make people buy a product. Whether the advertising is on the front of a store

November 23, 1987
Tobacco Products
indicating that it sells a particular brand or whether arts and culture is subsidized by a particular brand announcing a golf tournament, the ultimate benefit for the tobacco company is an increase in their sales.
I have some difficulty in believing that tobacco companies will continue to fund those organizations, using their names in big letters, with the expectation that no one will buy their product in return. That is a little hard to swallow.

Madam Speaker, of course advertising is done to make products better known and to get more people to buy them. Elowever, it also has another purpose, that is, to tell what is sold in a store.
If I am going to buy cigarettes I do not want to have to go to half a dozen stores to find one that sells them. If you have no intention of buying cigarettes, a sign in a store saying that it sells cigarettes will not encourage you to smoke. In my view, that is not at all the same as picturing someone whom we consider to be a hero, such as an aircraft pilot, smoking a cigarette. In my view that is entirely different. It is suggesting that that man is a pilot because he smokes.
I believe that there is a difference between lifestyle advertising and simply an indication that something is sold in a store. It may well encourage people who want to buy cigarettes to enter the store, but I do not think it will encourage someone who wants to buy a chocolate bar to buy a package of cigarettes instead.

Madam Speaker, I have an observation rather than a question. The Minister's office has sent me a number of brochures relating to the Government's effective campaign for educating our young population through the schools. I want to thank the officials of the Minister's office who kindly sent that material to me in the last minutes.
There should be wider use of this kind of information. In addition to sending it to MPs there should be co-operation with school boards across the country. Rather than receiving one of these on my desk I would like my children and all children to receive this information at school. There is no doubt that my children will have this package of information tonight, but I would like all young people to receive the same kind of encouragement, not only to quit smoking for those who do, but not to start for those who have not yet had the unfortunate experience of partaking in the weed.

Madam Speaker, I fully agree with the Hon. Member. I believe we should begin education at the earliest possible grade.
I recall teaching eleven grades at Churchill school just outside Drumheller. We had a health period three times a week. To my knowledge, not one student in that class smoked. I recall one of my students suggesting a way to show that it may be wrong to smoke. This student suggested that the class be shown a picture of the lungs of a non smoker, then depict
what the lungs look like after smoking for a year, and what they look like after 50 years of smoking.
I thought this was an excellent idea and said that I would obtain a picture of the lungs for the class project. I asked this student why he wanted to do this project. He told me that his father had been smoking for 50 years. His father said that it never hurt him, but his mother said that it does affect him. He wanted to show his father what it was doing to his lungs because he wanted him to live for a long time.
The pictures that this student drew were so realistic that I do not believe any youngster in that school ever smoked after seeing them. The majority of students I have met since that time do not smoke and most of them say it is due to the class project which showed the effect of smoking on lungs after 50 years. I believe it is important to provide such education in the school to the greatest possible degree. I believe that is where we will obtain the greatest results.

Madam Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to give you some of my personal impressions on Bill C-51. I think we all tend to applaud virtue and discourage vice. Now is smoking a vice, a way to relax or a habit? I think only the user knows for sure.
I am not so sure I agree with the ban on advertising, and I have my own personal opinion in this respect. When people say that advertising is dangerous for young people, for adults and for anyone who might want to start smoking or who already smokes, 1 am not so sure people are being realistic, if we look at how young people react. I am thinking of my own experience, in fact, I have been going through this almost daily, every week.
Every time I give my assistant's little boy a ride in my car, all hell breaks loose. I smoke and he doesn't. He rolls down the window, and we have a big argument. Sometimes I get to the point where I stop the car and tell him: I have a right to smoke. If you don't like it, you can get out. And this kid is exposed to all kinds of advertising, in magazines, in newspapers and cigarette commercials. Nowadays, kids are being educated to realize that smoking may be dangerous and that smoking is bad for them. We don't even have to tell them. We don't have to explain. It is part of growing up today, and kids are being taught, and they learn very quickly, that cigarettes may be harmful.
I fail to see why we should make it even more complicated. Tobacco companies and cigarette manufactures know perfectly well that some day, measures will be taken to prevent as many people as possible from smoking, or at least enable nonsmokers to live a better life than smokers.
They are prepared to co-operate, and I know about this from Imperial Tobacco. They came to see me and said they had presented a brief to the Minister about ways of controlling their own industry. I looked at their suggestions, and I felt they were very sensible. They were imposing very strict self-
November 23, 1987

censorship, but instead of that, we get this Bill, and personally, I never heard anyone say that we absolutely needed this legislation to prevent advertising and to prevent people from smoking. As you know, cigarette companies and tobacco companies, whatever they happen to sell, are major participants in regional and local economies. They invest huge sums of money in golf tournaments, cultural events and sports activities. People say that if they advertise, they must want to sell more. JTowever, they know as well as we do, that you can show a non-smoker any cigarette brand you want, but it won't make him want to smoke.
Advertising is specifically targeted at the user. Whether you are using one brand of cigarettes or another, it will try to convince you to switch. Sometimes, the same company which manufactures different brands of cigarettes will push one to compete with another. Personally, I think this is allright. I do not see why we should stop these companies from investing in advertising campaigns to encourage people to try their different brands. I can say that I never smoked a cigarette until I was 29 years old; it was not because of advertising in magazines or on TV-it seems to me that there were no longer any TV ads then-it was not because people forced me, but simply that one day, as an adult, I decided that I wanted to try. I liked it, and I continued.
It is a fact that today, as a consumer, I am interested in advertising; they try to convince us, in a thousand ways- colour of packaging, stronger or weaker cigarettes-that one brand is superior to another. I am affected to a certain extent, but I do not feel bad about it, for as a smoker, I should be tempted to watch the ad and learn more about the product, which is not always the case.
What worries me is the kind of money that will be lost. I am concerned about this Bill because of the money which will be lost and which would have been invested in a great many community projects. For instance, when I was young, I was involved in bicycle competitions. We were in need of funds for cycling which, as a European sport, was not very well known here. We needed funds to travel to places where we could practice our sport. A funny thing is that the government of Quebec asked a cigarette manufacturing company to pay for our travel to Europe to practice our sport without having any trade name on our T-shirt, without being told that we had to promote everywhere that such and such company was sponsoring us and making it possible for us to take part in an event. At the time, there were 16 of us, all under 16 years of age, who benefited not from an advertising campaign, but at least from a service to the community.
I cannot understand why the government insists on imposing such a legislation. It is a fact that in my Verdun-Saint-Paul riding, Imperial Tobacco employees are very nervous. They are worried about losing their jobs if there is a ban on advertising. However, that is not really the problem, because the number of smokers is decreasing. On the other hand, we have to provide enough time for these companies to find a new market and for these workers to find another job instead of scaring them by simply saying that there will be no more advertising or selling of cigarettes and that there is a ban on smoking. In my region,
Tobacco Products
the industry represents 800 people, or three or four people in each family, which means 2,500 people will be directly affected, and this does not include the advertising companies.
What most concerns me is that we might be a bit too drastic in making our decisions. I smoke myself and I am not ashamed of it. At times, I find that the non-smoker is much more bothersome than the smoker because you are treated like a monster if you take out a cigarette in public places. We seem to have virtually lost the right to smoke. There is no need to ban advertising to show us that we are doing something wrong. We have only to look in the eyes of the non-smokers to realize that we are no longer wanted. For my part, I believe that we have to give a chance to the people and the companies. Canada is a free country. These people have rights, and I personally have a lot of difficulty in supporting the Bill because every company is entitled to advertise and have its presence felt on the market, whether it is a tobacco company or some other business. We could say that most people die in their own beds.
Are we going to ban beds? There are a thousand such examples. What I would ask the committee to which this Bill will be referred to do, is not to say that there will be a ban on advertising. Why should we not provide a bit more time for the workers, the advertising companies and the members of the industry to adjust? I believe that people would be much happier if they were not being told that they cannot do such or such a thing, but if they were simply given advice to follow if they want, because if people tell us that smoking will kill us, it remains our own choice. Banning cigarettes or cigarette advertising will not make me change my mind about smoking.

Madam Speaker, I have a few comments to make about the speech of the Hon. Member. I believe that he raised a very important point when he spoke about advertising. We can ask ourselves whether advertising makes people smoke more. There is no advertising for marijuana. There is no advertising for cocaine or heroin, yet a lot of people, especially young people, use these drugs. This seems to show that advertising has no direct relation with consumption. There is perhaps some link, but no direct relationship. 1 believe that what we need is information. Today, our young people smoke more than before and women smoke more than they used to because of the stress of modern life and emancipation. Women want to be equal to men and young people want to appear older than they are. I think this is why our young people smoke. It is not because someone told them that smoking is popular.
The point I wish to raise concerns the freedom of expression. Would we restrict the freedom of expression by banning advertising? I believe that this is the threat inherent in this Bill. The only thing to do is to ensure freedom of expression. It is essential in a democratic society. What I wonder is whether this Bill does not restrict freedom of expression. A self-respecting democratic society should not be afraid of freedom of expression. For instance, if people drink or eat too much, it

Tobacco Products
can certainly be as harmful as smoking. We all know that obesity causes certain problems. Overeating causes obesity and obesity causes high blood pressure, which is certainly dangerous. The only answer is to inform the public that all abuses are dangerous.
The same is true for tobacco. If the public is told that abuses are dangerous, we shall realize that most people are reasonable. We can see it right now. Many people do not smoke because they are well-informed. People also watch what they eat because they know that it is dangerous to overeat. They also know that it is bad to drink too much. Everything must be done in moderation. On the other hand, I believe that we are certainly restricting freedom of thought by passing a Bill to ban advertising. And, as I said, freedom of expression is an essential element in a democratic society.
Indeed the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) had raised that point and said that freedom must be respected in a democratic society.
As a physician I would surely have seen the harmful effects of abuses-eating abuses, drinking abuses, or smoking abuses-and what people need is to lead a healthful life, exercise regularly, refrain from eating and smoking too much, sleep normal hours, and all this is bound to have an effect on our health.
Simply saying that advertising will be banned does not mean that abuses will be curbed. As I said before, some people take drugs-as a physician, for example, I saw people who reach for a cigarette when they feel nervous, but if a cigarette is not handy they will take drugs. Is it better to take drugs or to smoke? That is the question I am asking myself.
For this reason I am against the Bill as drafted because it does restrict advertising as well as individual freedom of expression, and I would suggest that what we need is information. Information can only come from one source: education, and that has to begin on school benches, as the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) put it: School is the source of information. If youngsters are told that too much smoking, eating or drinking is not good for them and that they must have healthy habits, then we will have a healthy society. That is certainly not the kind of thing the state can impose. The state can tell people smoking is harmful, have warnings printed on packages of cigarettes to the effect that it is a health hazard-

He was told that if he continued, he would be dead in three years. It did not stop me from smoking and I continue to smoke even today.

ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING NATIONAL OBJECTIVES Hon. J. Robert Howie (York-Sunbury) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of establishing, through joint negotiations with the provinces, national objectives in education including, but without limiting the generality of the foregoing, quantitative medium and long-term targets for a reduction in the rate of illiteracy on both a national and a provincial basis;
That the government examine the benefits of establishing a national council on education to promote the jointly negotiated and agreed upon national objectives; and
That within the general framework of a national interest in education, the provinces be free to act as they see fit to meet these national objectives and to achieve the targeted reductions in illiteracy.
He said: Madam Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is to acknowledge, at one and the same time, the constitutional priority of the provinces and the vital responsibilities of the federal Government in the education of our adult population.
The urgent challenges which both levels of government must confront range across the entire spectrum. At one extreme, recent studies have revealed an alarmingly high rate of adult illiteracy, a handicap which condemns its victims to a helpless existence on the margins of Canadian economic life. Both the personal suffering of such individuals and the cost they represent to society demand that Governments act quickly and decisively against the problem.
At the opposite end of the spectrum, our universities have clearly arrived at a crisis in terms of their ability to produce the quality of researchers and research necessary to maintain Canada's competitiveness in the world economy. With or without freer trade with the United States, our ability to match brains with the rest of the industrialized world will ultimately determine whether we can achieve the goals of social justice and humanity which all of us want.
In between these extremes we have a system of public school, community college, and university education which, if not teetering on the brink of collapse, finds it increasingly difficult to meet our many expectations. We expect it to provide students with a bewildering array of advanced technical and social knowledge and skills. We expect it to provide equal access and a reasonable chance of success to members of traditionally disadvantaged groups. We expect it to adapt quickly to changes in the workplace and to respond to new social priorities. We expect it to do these things, however, in a context of increasing class size and deteriorating buildings, equipment, and libraries.
Although the national importance of education has been recognized at least since the end of the Second World War, the history of federal-provincial co-operation is not one in which either level of government should take pride. There is little to be gained at this stage by assessing blame. It must be recognized, however, that there remains a legacy of mutual suspicion which must be overcome if we are to meet the contemporary challenge. We in this federal Parliament have no business lecturing the provinces about their responsibilities or attempting to dictate the form of future co-operation.
However, we can and should commit our Parliament and Government of Canada to principles such as the following: moral and material support for common approaches taken with the provinces, either individually or collectively through the Council of Ministers of Education, to national problems such as adult illiteracy and the access of traditionally disadvantaged groups to post-secondary education; substantially increased support for the research capacity and activity of our universities, provided in a manner which respects the priorities of the institutions and the provinces; and creation, upon consultation and agreement with all provinces, of a permanent mechanism or mechanisms to determine national objectives and ensure the co-ordination of federal and provincial efforts in post-secondary education.
The motion I have presented to the House stresses the issue of illiteracy for a number of reasons. First, in a society as affluent and well educated as ours, the current magnitude of the problem is a national disgrace. Second, since adult illiteracy is not a subject to which either level of government has traditionally paid much attention, there are no jurisdictional jealousies or vested interests. The way is clear for immediate, co-operative action.
However, I would not hide the fact that the intent of the motion is much broader. Successful action on this first front must serve as a model and inspiration for broader initiatives. Participants at the national forum on post-secondary education in Saskatoon achieved a remarkable degree of consensus on the proper goals and priorities of the educational system. Whether the "spirit of Saskatoon" survives the difficult and intricate process of finding the right means depends in large measure on the quality and sincerity of our political leadership. The intent of the motion is for the House to begin showing the way.

In concluding I should like to mention some positive measures which I feel have been taken in the right direction. In October 1986, for the first time in history, illiteracy received mention in the Speech from the Throne. Last year the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) declared war on illiteracy in our prisons, and in the past few months the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) has introduced significant new measures, including the establishment of a national literacy secretariat, the appointment of a national literacy council, increased funding of community programs, and an extension of federal-provincial co-operation in literacy initiatives.
The national forum on post-secondary education, which was an excellent success, was held after my motion was introduced, and the subject is now being studied by the Standing Committee on Secretary of State. This necessitates a technical change in my motion, so I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain):
That the word "government" be deleted in paragraphs 1 and 2 and be
replaced by: "Standing Committee on Secretary of State"
I seek unanimous consent of the House to make this change.
