seems to me that the Hon. Member's motion complements that nicely. Indeed it supports the general idea that we have national problems in Canada which call for national solutions.
He is quite right that although education is a provincial responsibility-and we all recognize that; nobody would want to take away that responsibility-we have too many serious national problems which can only be addressed by a national consensus.
It is my feeling that in unity there is strength and that, instead of having to go it alone, the provinces can go it cooperatively with their sister provinces, with the Government of Canada, and possibly with other members of the educational constituency-students, teachers, and administrators who are interested in it.
The motion of the Hon. Member focuses particularly on literacy. I think it is commendable because it is a serious blot on the national face. There is no question that illiteracy is a serious problem all across the country ranging from British Columbia to Newfoundland. Illiteracy in the population goes anywhere from just below 20 per cent, as I recall the figures in British Columbia, to a high of over 40 per cent in the Province of Newfoundland. In between, in Ontario and Quebec, we have percentages in the twenties.
Whether illiteracy is 18 per cent or 44 per cent of the population, it is completely unacceptable from a moral point and an economic point of view. I understand there will very soon be a study being done on the question of illiteracy which will show that not only is this a human problem creating a tragic difficulty for individuals but it is costing our country hundreds of millions of dollars. I have not even dealt with the safety aspect of the person who cannot read signs on the job. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who cannot participate fully in Canadian life because they cannot read and write and are not functional. It costs businesses hundreds of millions of dollars. I suggest that those businesses have to take a look at this as must the Government.
I feel that the Government has not made the kind of commitment it should. A million dollars to solve the problem of illiteracy is almost an insult. It is little better than that. It will need many more dollars before we can say that we have made an adequate contribution to the problem of illiteracy.
I agree with the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury that these things should be done jointly. But it should not be just a federal and provincial effort. We must go beyond that. The Member went beyond that by suggesting that we need, I think the words he used to describe it are, a national council on education. In part his motion reads:
That the Government examine the benefits of establishing a national council
on education to promote the jointly negotiated and agreed upon national
objectives-
He goes beyond the motion of Friday which dealt with postsecondary education. The Canadian Teachers' Federation, for

November 23, 1987
Education
example, has had for quite some time a policy asking for exactly what the Hon. Member proposes in his motion.
1 believe with the Hon. Member that it is time now not to look at things as we always have historically. When the country was put together in 1867 there were certain realities in Canada. It seems to me that we are still living with the structures put in place in 1867, but this is 1987. Perhaps we need a new, fresh vision of what it is to be Canadian and how we can get people to participate in national life fully. I agree with the general thrust of what the Hon. Member is saying. There is in Canada now a national need.
He is quite right in saying that not only is illiteracy a problem but that the problem ranges all the way to postsecondary education. The post-secondary education system in Canada has been described as being in crisis. I do not think that is an understatement. There is the question of underfunding, the question of limited assets, the question of teachers and professors who are leaving for the United States, and the question of professors who are not being replaced. The 40 or 50 year old professor is not being replaced because many people are not entering the field of university teaching. Salaries are low.
In my own Province of Newfoundland if you walk through the tunnels between the buildings at Memorial University you will find drips all the way through from the plant pipes. Normal maintenance has not been done. Our university buildings and facilities are falling into disrepair. This is a serious problem. It cannot be the responsibility of the provinces alone. In the Province of Newfoundland, if I can take that example again, there is not the financial adequacy within the budget to deal with these problems, particularly if federal funding is being cut back. The provinces which this motion and approach would help are the less well off provinces in Canada. Ontario can probably well survive on its own and deal with this problem. It is doing so, as is Quebec. I have to say quite candidly in this Chamber that most of the outstanding initiatives in Canada that have taken place within the recent past have come out of the Province of Quebec.
From a financial point, strategy and policy point of view, Ontario and Quebec are handling their problems, I think, in an imaginative way. That is not true for the provinces not in the same financial position. It seems to me that a co-ordinated cooperative national approach would help. We need a national vision to help the disadvantaged particularly. Whether we are talking about disadvantaged people or disadvantaged regions, we need to band together, to create not a federal or provincial body but a national body to deal with the very powerful, important, tragic and imminent national need.
I have a great deal of pleasure in supporting the motion of the Member from York-Sunbury, and I compliment the Hon. Member for bringing it forward. He has mentioned a couple of other things that I have not because of time constraints. He is quite right that there must be adequate funds for research. He
mentioned that illiteracy is the most urgent problem and that there should be broader initiatives later on.
I support this motion and I believe my Party as a whole will support it. It is something that should not be dropped. It should be kept very much alive. I hope there will be an opportunity within the House and within the committee of the Secretary of State to examine this fundamental problem from the ground up, ranging from illiteracy to post-secondary education. We cannot put it aside. We must deal with it, and I hope the House will see in its wisdom that that is the case and support the motion of the Hon. Member.

Madam Speaker, I rise to support the motion of the Hon. Member for York- Sunbury (Mr. Howie). It is very similar to a motion I submitted which has not been called for debate. My motion reads as follows:
That a special committee of the House should be established to consider
Canada's serious and growing illiteracy problem and recommend ways that the
Government, in conjunction with the provinces and territories, can join the
United Nations attack on illiteracy.
It is frightening, to say the least, that a country as industrially developed as Canada finds that almost a quarter of its people are functionally illiterate. An in-depth series on the problem and the scope of it was reported in a number of articles that appeared in Southam newspapers within the last year describing the dimensions of the problem. A study indicated that 24 per cent of Canadians are functionally illiterate. That are five million people and 13 per cent of these are recent high school graduates. In a study done for the Canadian Association of Adult Education in June 1985, it was reported that in the Provinces of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, and Quebec more than one in four adults have less than a Grade 8 education. Almost 40 per cent of Canadian women and almost 35 per cent of Canadian men with less than a Grade 8 education live in Quebec. One-third of the educationally disadvantaged adults are employed. Seven per cent are unemployed, and the unemployment rate is 15 per cent. Three-fifths are not in the labour force; that is, are not actively seeking work.
This is a problem which has tremendous and profound implications for all Canadians. Like most other countries in the world, we are moving to an era in which education and knowledge are an absolute necessity if our citizens are to find the kind of jobs which will be available. Increasingly, these jobs will call for a much better level of education than most of us have, and particularly for a better education than those who are functionally illiterate have.
One of the problems is that we have never really faced up to asking who are the functionally illiterate. If we did ask that question, we would find that the groups from which the illiterate come vary from province to province and from city to city. In most larger cities, there are new immigrants who came from countries in which the languages spoken were neither
November 23, 1987

English nor French. In some cities such as Winnipeg or Regina, there are native people who have moved in recent years from the reserves where education was, by any standard that can be set, deficient to say the least. There are people who grew up and lived in rural areas where until very recently the educational standards were very low.
It is good news that the federal Conservative Government has recognized the problem publicly and has allocated $1 million to fight illiteracy. However, looking at the scope of the problem, we realize that the amount allocated is a mere a drop in the bucket. As I see it, it is merely a public relations exercise.
Ian Morrison, the Director of the Canadian Association for Adult Education, has estimated that it would take $100 million to substantially improve literacy in Canada. It is pretty clear that without major efforts on the part of Governments, both federal and provincial, in co-operation with the groups in various parts of Canada which have worked on the problem and learned how to help people who are illiterate, real progress will not be made.
Organizations such as Frontier College, the Regina Public Library and unions in my city such as the International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union, all have programs ongoing. These programs are small but these organizations have learned a great deal about how to begin to cope with the problem. However, $1 million will not do very much. We cannot expect the provinces or the cities to do the job which is required if for no other reason than that they simply do not have the money.
Just last week, there was a small article in the Toronto Star reporting that school districts in Toronto and North York are having tremendous problems. There has been a tremendous influx of immigrant students who need education in English as a second language. These school boards do not have the financial ability to deal with those problems.
We need a new approach, we need a serious approach. Some months ago, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) announced a program to help those in penitentiaries who are illiterate to get an education. 1 welcome that program, but 1 ask why it is restricted only to people who are in penitentiaries.
The Department of Employment and Immigration under the former Liberal Government and under the present Government has cut back on programs which can be described as adult basic education. Those are the programs which could help a great many illiterate people. However, the Departments have not been very sympathetic to this idea. They have been cutting back on those programs because no quick results are shown. People do not get jobs if they only have this basic educational training funded by the Department of Employment and Immigration. The Department wants to show that people who participate in its programs move quickly into jobs.
The reality is that people who are functionally illiterate are almost always either unemployed or have low-paying unskilled
Education
jobs from which they will never be able to move. It is clear that a major effort must be made in this regard.
It is true that this federal Government, like the former Liberal Government, takes the attitude that education under our Constitution is a provincial responsibility and therefore the federal Government very frequently refuses to get involved and to put up money. People who are illiterate are doomed to failure in the future. That failure will be felt by those people first but it will be felt by all Canadians as well.
We in Canada have one of the worst records of any of the industrialized countries in the world. It seems to me that we need a decision made by the federal Government to co-operate with the provinces and the voluntary agencies which have experience in this area to assess the dimensions of the problem and calculate the costs of improving the situation. There has been no real improvement in the situation in the last 25 years. The percentage of the functionally illiterate has hovered at between 20 per cent and 25 per cent and is not getting lower despite all the supposed efforts made by the federal Government, by the provinces and by the voluntary agencies. All of these efforts together have been less than successful.
We need a commitment from the federal Government to cooperate with the provinces in calculating the methods that can be used to reduce the number of functionally illiterate and the costs of this. The federal Government must agree to participate in the battle. That means that it must participate in the funding of a major effort.
While I welcome this resolution, I am not too hopeful that the federal Government, given its concentration on the need to control or reduce the deficit, is likely to do what is necessary. To the extent that this resolution helps highlight the dimensions of the problem, I support it.

Madam Speaker, whether or not this should be a political issue is a question which I do not wish to discuss. I do not believe that the first two speakers approached the political aspects in any way and I do not think we should do so in this debate.
Perhaps if the Government of Canada has made mistakes throughout Confederation, it may very well be that we have made too many political decisions without considering the practicality of them. I believe this is one decision that should now be and should stay above the rank of politics or its consideration as a political matter.
We do have a federal provincial confederation system of government. That system has delineated certain responsibilities to certain levels of government. I believe that if the federal Government has a level of responsibility, it is in influence and not in participation or interference. That is our responsibility.
I want to speak on this subject from the perspective of my experience as a student and teacher. I believe that if we are to exert influence, it may be along the lines of putting more

November 23, 1987
Education
emphasis on the three r's, reading, 'riting and 'rithmetic. Arithmetic, of course, is not a matter of literacy but it is very important.
When we speak about the incapacity of the illiterate, that incapacity is a handicap as real as a physical handicap in today's world. It has always been a handicap, but today it is a major handicap. I believe we have to come back to a much greater emphasis in our schools on reading and writing to the point that the first objective of education is competence in those two areas.
Over the years we have overlooked this as we accepted the representations of many people who had what they thought were compassionate ideas for teaching. Some of those ideas were that we should perhaps not have examinations or competition, but we should allow students to learn at the rate at which they wish to learn rather than at the rate at which they are capable of learning. I believe that some of the standards we have established for advancement from grade to grade have been such that students find themselves in a very handicapped position. We have ignored reading and writing to that point.
Not very long ago I talked to a student who graduated from high school at the honours level only to find that she had taken courses which in no way prepared her for college. Yet college had been her declared goal for years. The practice of her school was to emphasize subjects other than those which provide a broad base of information and knowledge to put you in a position to be competent in college. That is where we have to provide some leadership and influence. However, we should not take action which will interfere in any way with a sphere of provincial jurisdiction as important as this one is.
1 had the experience of becoming a teacher at the same high school I attended. By that time a curriculum was in place different from that which I experienced as a student. When I was a student I had to write essays, create stories and write letters, which were in turn examined and graded by the teacher. When I became a parent no such practice was followed with my children.
I have employed people in my office who graduated from high school or business college and could not spell. I mean they could not spell in a very rudimentary way. Yet they had graduated and become secretaries.
When 1 began teaching in Grade 9 I found that I now had a student body which could not read or understand high school textbooks because there had been a major change in the vocabulary requirement in the first eight grades of school.
If we have a responsibility here it is to provide leadership. We must restore to the school system competence in reading and writing as a necessary basis for promotion from class to class. Let us not have poor spellers coming out of high school and business colleges seeking employment. No, they are not illiterate but the education system has obviously been negligent
in extending to those students the skills so necessary for the occupation they have chosen.
I understand that the Hon. Member for Grand Falls- White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) was a teacher. I do not know what experience he might have had but he spoke as one with a sincere interest in education, as have other speakers.
I congratulate the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) for putting this motion before the House and I congratulate those who have participated in the debate. I hope that we give this subject consideration which is completely unprejudiced and unpolitical.
If this motion goes to committee we will not be pestered by special interest groups. Our consideration will be dedicated to the best interests of all Canadians with respect to our education system. Let us hope that we elevate that system to the point that when one leaves high school one can listen to media commentary or read The Globe and Mail or The Telegraph-Journal with understanding and comprehension.
There are degrees of illiteracy. There are those who cannot read or write at all. However, the degree of literacy we must achieve is that which will allow the young people of this nation to move into whatever career they choose with the ability to use their skills in the best possible way. Without that capability, those people are handicapped. It must be costing us not millions but billions in lost productivity.
The best educated people in the world today, presumably, are the Japanese and they are leading the way. It used to be that the United States had the highest number of high school graduates, college graduates and technical school graduates. I do not believe that applies any longer. Therefore, let us step up the level of advice from Government so there will no longer be illiterates and our graduate students at whatever level will be more competent in developing both our society and their own future than they are today.

Madam Speaker, first, I would like to say that I really appreciate the Private Member's motion introduced by the hon. Member for York- Sunbury (Mr. Howie). I believe that it is very important. It is unacceptable that we should have such a high rate of illiteracy in our society.

I would like to tell the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) as well as the Hon. Member for Grand Falls- White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) that the level of illiteracy in our society is totally unacceptable. The figures run from one in five to one in four, so you can imagine what the total effect must be on the social, economic, political and moral interests of all Canadians. This is a national disgrace and needs very serious attention.
November 23, 1987

I appreciate the suggestion made by the Member to move for a national council on education to promote jointly negotiated and agreed upon national objectives. However, it will take a great deal of time to arrive at such a federal-provincial initiative. We must consider some creative and innovative solutions in the interim. Notwithstanding the fact that I totally support any initiative, we need some other mechanisms until we are able to address this problem fully.
As a director of youth protection in the Province of Quebec I noted with a great deal of sadness the discomfort, embarrassment, and unwillingness of parents to acknowledge their illiteracy. They could not read contracts which were written for their children who had performed criminal acts and were in the first stage of becoming non-productive members of our society. These parents were incapable of understanding the contents of written contracts. These people love their children and want to help them, yet are unable to do so in acute situations. What must happen on a daily basis when they want to lend a hand in the general education of their children?
The level of illiteracy is a reflection of the level of immigration to this country and the fact that we have not done a good job of integration with new immigrants who are the backbone of the building of this country. If we want new immigrants to become well established and able to make the contributions which they need to make to society we must make a commitment from the first day that they come to this land.
The first commitment is to ensure that every man, woman, and child who comes here is at least able to read, write and know the fundamentals of our language in order that they can do their banking and shopping and understand a contract with a landlord. It is absolutely crucial from a social perspective that these people be able to understand our society. If they become ill they must be able to follow medical instructions and read labels on medication. The implications are very serious because these people are incapacitated and handicapped. If we looked at it in that way we would be able to move in a number of areas other than only through the Department of Immigration.
I am not trying to politicize this debate, but I believe that the $1 million which the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) has seen fit to allocate right now is only a small drop in the bucket. I tend to agree with the Adult Education Association of Canada that we need hundreds of millions of dollars.
I would like to suggest one creative stop-gap measure which has been researched and has proven very effective. It is with relation to open captioning on television. That little square box in our home has a very important impact on our lives. Everyone who watches this box can learn effectively. By watching the lettering at the bottom of the screen people learn by associating the word with the image.
The hearing impaired have complained that less than 50 per cent of the programs which they would like to watch are close-
Education
captioned and that their rights are abridged under the Constitution. They believe they should be able to watch all programs. I suggest that, as a start, all news programs should be close captioned because we become good citizens by understanding what is going on in our society. By running open captioning we could render a service to the hearing impaired and the illiterate at the same time. We would be accomplishing at least one step toward the multitude of action plans which will be required. We need creative, innovative, and imaginative ideas.
People are ashamed and embarrassed to acknowledge that they have been in this wonderful county for many years but have not been able to master either English or French. They may not be illiterate in their own language, but in Canada they are illiterate with regard to the economic, social, and political impact on their lives and on our country.
I make that suggestion as one window of opportunity on the national objective. I believe that we should look more closely at the handling of immigrants and their integration into our society. I refer not only to the working men and women and their children, but also to the husband or wife who chooses to work at home. That is very important.
I am sure that no Member of this House is proud of the fact that some 20 to 25 per cent of our society is in those circumstances. This is a cumulative problem and we must begin now to push the project ahead. I congratulate the Hon. Member on the project and let us accomplish some other things at the same time.

Madam
Speaker, as Chairperson of the House of Commons Standing Committee on the Secretary of State I am extremely pleased at the prospect of our committee taking on the subject matter of the motion of the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie). I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for raising issues which affect literally millions of Canadians from all walks of life, all age groups, and all sectors of our society. I hope that within the next few minutes there will be unanimous consent to refer this matter to the Standing Committee on Secretary of State.
It is very clear that the Government fully supports the spirit of the motion. Through the Department of the Secretary of State, and especially the Minister, the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), the Government has worked hard to put education issues on the national agenda. I want to pay tribute at this time to the Secretary of State who showed imagination and courage in mounting the national forum in post-secondary education in Saskatoon. I will have a few more words to say about that in a moment.

I am glad to see that the motion recognizes the constitutional jurisdiction of the provinces for education. We all know that the educational system comes under provincial jurisdiction,

November 23, 1987
Education
and all federal initiatives in this area must take this fact into account.
Members of this House are well aware that federal contributions are mostly for post-secondary education. Leaving aside the urgent problem of illiteracy, the Government has given priority to many problems which require an immediate attention.
These concerns were discussed, as I was saying earlier, at the historic three-day national forum on post-secondary education held in Saskatoon from October 25 to October 27. It was historic because that was the first time that the federal and provincial Governments have co-sponsored such a national educational event. It was historic because it brought together not only both federal and provincial Governments, but academics and people from all walks of life who care about higher education.
The forum provided a chance for the first truly national exploration of the challenges and opportunities of higher education in Canada. A gathering of more than 600 people represented the richness and diversity not only of Canada's colleges and universities, but also of Canadian society itself.

One of the major objectives of the Forum was to achieve a new national consensus on the importance of post-secondary education in Canada. The participants agreed that one of the major issues in that area was access for people of all ages and all cultural and linguistic groups.
Among the other concerns raised during the Forum to which the Government is giving its full attention, I would mention assistance to students through the Canadian Student Loans Program, the new incentive provisions for foreign students and university research.
The Secretary of State has asked for a full review of the Canadian Student Loans Program. This includes the creation of an ongoing intergovernmental advisory committee for student assistance and of a public advisory group, which will provide guidance on the future of federal programs in that area.

In addition, the Government has made known that it intends to make it easier and fairer for students to repay their loans, to improve assistance offered to part-time students, and to respond to the needs of the working poor, single parents and others with special needs.
In terms of increased accessibility, foreign students must also be included. Institutions as well as federal and provincial Governments recognize such students as assets and an investment in international good will. The Government has therefore recently announced the creation of 1,000 new
scholarships for foreign students from developing countries, bringing the total to 7,000, no imposition of a student visa fee, and an easing of the rules about foreign students working in Canada.

Madam Speaker, university research is another area where the Government has already shown a strong political will. Several weeks ago, the Government injected an additional $11 million into this year's budget for university research subsidy councils, as well as an additional $7 million for microelectronics research in universities.
Federal Government support to these councils now amounts to $600 million a year. The Government also developed recently a matching subsidy policy to promote Canadian private sector support.
However, a tragic problem still remains, that of illiteracy. Those who can neither read nor write sufficiently to accomplish the basic exchanges of daily life are truly disadvantaged in many ways. Innumerable communications means are closed to them and they are subject to constant humiliations.
The Secretary of State, who has been designated as the lead Minister responsible for the federal Government's literacy initiatives, issued a statement on September 8 to mark World Literacy Day. In his statement he outlined various initiatives which the federal Government is taking to give effect to the commitment made in the Throne Speech concerning literacy. The Minister emphasized a partnership approach with the provinces and with groups in the public and private sectors which are involved with this crucial problem.
I see that we are approaching the end of Private Members' Hour, Madam Speaker. In view of the sense in the Chamber on the part of all Parties that the motion of the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury be referred to the Standing Committee on Secretary of State, which committee I have the honour to chair, I request that the question now be put.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I note that the Hon. Member for London-Middlesex (Mr. Clifford) is out of the Chamber temporarily. Perhaps we could proceed to the next question on the adjournment debate and deal with the Hon. Member's question at the end of the late show.
TRADE-FILM DISTRIBUTION INDUSTRY-FILM IMPORT LICENSING/BOOK PUBLISHING INDUSTRY

Madam Speaker, I am rising to continue discussion on a question regarding film distribution and free trade which I raised in the House a short while ago. Members of the House may recall that there was a task force on film distribution. We have a situation in which most Canadians, when they go to the cinema, watch American films. Some 97 per cent of the profit of film distribution goes outside the country to the United States and is reinvested in film production. Canadian films are not being shown. The money from film distribution that you and I pay when we go to the movies is not going into Canadian film producing, hiring Canadian writers, directors, actors, and technical people, but is going to the United States, to Hollywood, and providing jobs there.
Those facts have been known for a very long time, and as a result of this the Liberal Government preceding this Government was afraid to do anything about this. This Government had a task force on the subject, and the Raymond-Roth report came out a couple of years ago recommending a system of Canadian ownership of film distribution.
The Government was not quite prepared to go as far as Canadian ownership in film distribution. It preferred to think that the task force had not even recommended that. However, it did agree to bring in a Bill on film distribution that would make it a little easier for Canadians to get into the industry and have more control over film distribution in Canada. Mainly this would be done by a system of licences for film importing.
A Bill to that effect has been prepared. It is in the Department of Communications. I have seen a copy of it. It has been circulated, not properly, but it is around. We know that the work has been done, a Bill has been drafted, yet it has not been
Adjournment Debate
introduced. Why not? It so happens that in discussions on free trade this is a very touchy matter.
The President of the United States is a former actor, and he has been defending his friends in the film industry who would like to continue to milk Canadians of all their profits from film distribution and have them go to Hollywood instead of Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, Winnipeg, or any other places that produce films.
We would like to see more production in Canada. But it seems that film distribution has been a sacrificial lamb for the free trade discussions. If the Government had kept its word on culture and free trade, there would be no section on culture in the free trade agreement at all. In fact, there is a section, it is not a very long section, but there is one. It seems that the Bill on film distribution has been sacrificed to get some accommodation from the Americans on free trade and culture.
I remind you, Madam Speaker, that culture was on the bargaining table, and there were give-aways; there were giveaways in periodical publications, and there were assurances that Canada would not take further so-called protectionist measures to add to the list of trade irritants. What seems to be protectionism for the United States is for us absolutely vital in order to have independent cultural industries at all, because we do not have the same market size as the Americans do to appeal to. We must have our own particular measures to ensure that our industries are fostered, and Canadian artistic and creative people get jobs in Canada.
It is with some dismay that I learned that the Minister is still saying that the Bill will come in. In documents that have come out from the United States there have been comments that, in the free trade arrangements and the negotiations, the Canadians agreed to solve the problem of Jack Valenti of the American majors. His problem is that he wishes to keep that 97 per cent of profits from Canada and keep us down to 3 per cent, instead of having us increase and coming more and more to manage our own Canadian film industry, and have the money from movie-goers go to provide more jobs for Canadian creative people.
If the free trade agreement had excluded culture completely, we would not have had this in the synopsis. The United States recognizes the importance to Canada of maintaining its cultural identity. However, at the same time the United States wants to ensure that Canadian cultural policies do not constitute a discriminatory and unnecessary barrier to U.S. trade. They call it discrimination. Our promoting Canadian culture to them is discrimination, and Canada agreed to that. Recognizing Canadian sensitivities, the United States has agreed that certain cultural areas are not subject to specific provisions of the agreement. However, others are. Printing is, and we have seen measures in book publishing to have printing done in Canada, for example, in the case of Ontario, where books cannot be bought for school boards that are not authored and printed in Canada. This kind of arrangement

November 23, 1987
Adjournment Debate
would now be illegal under the free trade agreement. It would certainly mean a loss of jobs in the printing industry.
The agreement continues:
For its part, Canada has agreed that cultural measures it takes will not impair the benefits the United States would otherwise expect from the provisions of the agreement.
There is a provision for compensation if Canada should do that. In short, Canada has agreed, in the cultural negotiations as part of the free trade agreement, to give up certain rights in cultural areas and that if the Government takes action in the future-and we would want it to take action-we would have to expect retaliation. In other words, we would be agreeing in advance that the United States had a case for retaliation against us, which is unacceptable. I have raised the matter before, and I will continue to raise it.
We want to see whether the Government, in good faith, is sticking to its guns on film distribution. It should bring in a Bill without delay and should make very clear to the Americans that culture is not something to be bargained away, that compensation is not appropriate, that indeed printing is a cultural industry like many other cultural industries, and that we want to safeguard our culture in Canada by using all methods at our disposal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the Minister indicated in the House, the Government has stated all along that our cultural industries would be protected in any trade deal. From the outset the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) have said that our cultural industries would be exempt from the agreement, and indeed we have done just that.
As well, the Minister told the House on October 5 that the Government had indicated that it was prepared to create a separate market for film distribution rights and to ensure that Canadian independent distributors would have access to those rights. This intention still stands and has not been altered as part of the trade agreement. There is nothing in the free trade deal which prevents us from meeting this objective.
The Government has shown strong commitment to foster comprehensively the development of a healthy Canadian film industry, and we will continue to do so.
One problem facing our distribution sector has always been the lack of a distinct national market. The policy the Minister proposed last February will ensure that Canada is treated as a separate market.
Another problem has been the lack of adequate financing. We are very aware of the critical role distributors play in a healthy, well-balanced film industry, and we want to ensure that Canadian distributors have access to a fair share of the Canadian film market so that they can rechannel funds back into the film industry.
The Government is examining additional measures which will be of benefit to the Canadian distribution sector, and we are doing so by consulting with the film industry.
Also the Hon. Member raised a question with regard to the Baie Comeau policy on foreign investment in the publishing industry. I must repeat to the Hon. Member that cultural industries are excluded from the investment chapter of the trade agreement. Therefore, the Baie Comeau policy remains in effect.
The Minister said in the House on October 5 that not only has the Government succeeded in maintaining the application of the Baie Comeau policy to indirect acquisitions, but we have also negotiated an agreement on indirect acquisitions in the cultural industries generally. To quote from the agreement, it reads:
Canada undertakes that in the event that it requires the divestiture to Canadians of a U.S. controlled business in a cultural industry, as part of the review of an indirect acquisition of such a business, Canada will offer to purchase the business at fair, open market value as determined by an independent, impartial assessment.
The Canadian Government will then resell these industries to a Canadian purchaser. That is a big step forward.
On September 26, 1985 the Prime Minister said the following when the Government formally undertook the free trade initiative:
Our political sovereignty, our system of social programs, our commitment to fight regional disparities, our unique cultural identity, our special linguistic character-these are the essence of Canada. They are not at issue in these negotiations.
Canada has scored a great victory in its trade agreement with the United States which will be of benefit to the entire country. We have done so without undermining our cultural identity. In fact, we have protected our cultural policies and programs in the free trade agreement, and the Hon. Member should indeed be congratulating us.
MARINE TRANSPORTATION 1NDUSTRY/DELAY ALLEGED IN PROCEEDING WITH LEGISLATION/REQUEST THAT MINISTER NOT SIGN TRANSPORTATION ANNEX TO AGREEMENT

Madam Speaker, I should recall that when reserving the right to review the provisions of the Canada-United States Free-Trade Agreement, on the matter of Marine transportation the United States Senate caught the Canadian Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) with his pants down.
Indeed, on September 23, 1987, the Standing Committee on Regulations approved an amendment to the fast review rule requiring that the American Senate should approve or reject the agreement without any amendments. This means the US Senate now be empowered to amend the provisions of the agreement dealing with marine transportation. Given the
November 23, 1987

current situation the 56 US Senators and 233 Congressmen who have signed resolutions requesting that any provisions that might harm US shipping be deleted from the Canada-US Agreement, expect to convince the American administration that it should delete the provisions concerning marine transportation, for fear of seeing the whole agreement fall flat.
Judging by the second draft schedule received last week, the Reagan administration is taking that threat very seriously, much more so than our Canadian Minister of Transport who last Friday had to recognize he was powerless. Indeed, the last transportation draft provisions show Canadian shipping would be excluded from any new maritime transportation program such as the US Government supplies and goods preference.
The Canadian marine industry had planned to challenge the US merchant marine legislation, the 1920 Jones Act, a bill that has been there, not for 200 years as the Minister of Transport indicated Friday but since 1920, and that applies to all components of the American maritime industry. Now Canadian shipping companies are disappointed that the free trade agreement did not result as they had hoped in the drafting of a North American Jones Act which, according to Mr. Fred Pitre, Vice President of Canada Steamship Lines, would have combined the open character and flexibility of the Canada Shipping Act with the national security safeguards contained in the Jones Act.
Speaking on behalf of the Dominion Marine Association, its Chairman Mr. Norman Hall is asking that short of an overall free trade agreement on shipping, Canadian negotiators should at least look at the matter of discriminatory investment rules in the United States. At the present time an Americam shipping company can invest up to 100 per cent in a Canadian company and use a foreign-built vessel to transport goods from one port to another in Canada. Conversely a Canadian investor can acquire only 25 per cent of an American shipping company and must use nothing but ships built in the United States. Competition therefore is unfair and definitely not favourable to Canada's economy. So much for a flagrant disparity which will be set in concrete under the Reagan-Mulroney agreement.
On the other hand Canadian shipyards and their employees have every interest to ensure that Canadian shipping services be given the same protection as the American merchant marine under the Jones Act. Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association President Clarke is afraid that any softening of the protection provisions might give foreign-built vessels access to Canada, and he wants Canadian legislation to provide the same protection as the American law. Finally, the labour unions-Seafarers International Union and Merchant Service Guild-which represent 5,000-odd Canadian sailors share this point of view.
Both unions are deeply concerned that Canadian shipping activities might come under strong attack from renamed vessels operated by American equipment and crews.
While the American shipping industry was making very strong representations to prevent our merchant marine from
Adjournment Debate
gaining access to the American domestic market, the Government introduced Bill C-52 whose purpose was to ensure that shipping operations in Canadian waters would be the exclusive reserve of Canadian vessels.
On the other hand, when we discussed the legislation we emphasized the fact that allowing foreign shipping to become involved in marine transportation within or without Canada's inshore waters, for lack of available Canadian ships, was in fact a dangerous surrendering of marine transportation operation to foreign companies, especially American ones. On the other hand, it was perhaps still more proper to state as we did that the time was ill-chosen for this Conservative Government to introduce amendments to the Shipping Act, and that they should have done that much earlier in their term of office, that is in 1985 or even 1986. A few weeks later, the Minister of Transport indicated our view when he called for the suspension of the Legislative Committee hearings on Bill C-52 until the conclusion of the free trade agreement.
The problem now is very serious. In line with the American shipping companies' suggestions that any new act or any amendment to existing acts should provide national treatment to the other country, Canada should now, if Bill C-52 is passed, once the free trade agreement is ratified, grant national treatment to American shipping companies.
That is the problem we are facing, which means that this Conservative Government's negligence has endangered the possibility of a shipping act reform along the lines of national prerogatives, and is now running the risk of having American companies invade our marine industry because of the delays already incurred.
Last Friday the Minister, in answer to my questions, said the United States had refused to yield on some items. One of those items was marine transportation. In the worst case, the status quo would be maintained. But the status quo is unacceptable in the circumstances. All this points to the total failure of the Minister of Transport, who in the circumstances is seen as the worst Minister of Transport in Canada's history. He is famous for his jokes, but surely the Canadian transport industry is not laughing: it is shocked at this Minister's incompetence.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Government has been incorrectly accused of selling out the Canadian transportation industry for the sake of a free trade agreement with the United States. Let me assure Hon. Members that this is absolutely not the case.
I find it hard to believe that preserving the status quo can be misconstrued by Hon. Members opposite as a sell-out. We are not giving anything away. We argued for the easing up of restrictions on both sides of the border. We proposed cabotage

November 23, 1987
Adjournment Debate
in all modes of transport. Because the U.S. would not agree, there will be no roll-backs by either country.
We are anticipating that the agreement will result in a larger volume and a value of goods, services and people travelling in both directions. This should stimulate Canadian firms involved in transborder transport activity.
Canadian transportation firms are already competitive and they will be even more competitive under the new National Transportation Act and the new Motor Vehicle Transport Act. For several years now, Canadian trucking firms have enjoyed access to the U.S. market-place. These firms were quick to capitalize on the opportunity provided by U.S. deregulation and have successfully established themselves in the U.S. market.
In future, American carriers wishing to operate domestically in Canada will still be required to establish a Canadian subsidiary, to employ Canadians, to pay Canadian taxes and so on. It will be easier for them to obtain a licence, that is true, but in every other respect, customs and immigration laws apply as they do in the other way. In short, the same situation which has applied to Canadians in the U.S. market since 1980 will apply.
It is true that each state will be able to continue to regulate trucking within its borders. However, trucking associations which have been critical of the FTA have yet to cite even a single instance of a Canadian trucker being refused entry by a U.S. state. Not one example of this has been brought to our attention, and I would like to see one. I can only conclude from that that the problem is not as bad as they say it is.
Accusations have also been made that Bill C-18 has given American railway companies access to Canadian markets while the free trade agreement did not secure reciprocal access. Competitive line rates provisions of the National Transport Act were instituted to assist Canadian shippers captive to one railway, not to allow U.S. railways to access the Canadian market. These competitive line rates provisions can be suspended if Canadian railways suffer significant economic losses. In summary, the free trade agreement will be good for Canadians and good for the Canadian transportation industry.

Madam
Speaker, I certainly appreciate your consideration on this very hectic day.
On May 28, 1987, I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) how ordinary Canadians could have input on decisions being made by VIA Rail. Both the Minister and VIA Rail agreed that greater consultation between the corporation and the people it serves was needed.
Shortly after, on June 11, a new VIA consultative committee was established and its inaugural meeting was held in
London to discuss scheduling, service, marketing, equipment allocation, and other topics of interest to both VIA Rail and the municipalities it serves. The committee felt that VIA had a real problem with on-time performance and the resulting negative public perception of VIA. VIA reacted to those concerns in a positive way which is a good example of how, by working together, good things can be accomplished. Let me give you some examples.
In the first five months of 1986, the over-all average on-time performance of trains through London was 69 per cent. In the same five-month period in 1987 the average was 76 per cent. Then the on-time performance commitment program by VIA was put in place and even greater improvements were made. For May 1 to September 30, 1987, some 75 per cent of the trains travelling from Toronto to Windsor through London were on time. For trains from Toronto through London to Sarnia it was 83 per cent. It is interesting to note that 90 per cent of the trains from Toronto to London were on time. Clearly, the consultative committees and VIA working together produced a good result.
Given that, I wonder why the program was discontinued at the end of October. Perhaps even greater gains could have been realized had this program been maintained by VIA.
Another problem that the committee recognized was frequency of service. Both lines north and south of London have asked for a late train from Toronto. To date neither request has had a positive result. We cannot even get a late night train for weekend travel from Toronto to London and cities beyond. The committee has experienced some frustration there.
A new first-class service, VIA-1, was introduced in October and it has received very positive response in our community, particularly on the morning train. We have also realized very positive passenger trends recently. In southwestern Ontario passenger use is up 5.8 per cent over all this year, and on the Toronto-London-Windsor corridor it is up 11.7 per cent. It is very encouraging to see that VIA is listening to these communities and getting things done.
The most travelled corridor in Canada is the Windsor-Quebec City corridor. The City of London representative asked why the new equipment which VIA was able to get as a result of the actions of the Government would go to unprofitable runs, namely the transcontinental runs, rather than to the most travelled corridor in Canada where the prospects for profit were brightest. Why were we shut out? The London committee was quite concerned about VIA's action in this area.
More LRC equipment is not available because an LRC updating program is in progress. They are fixing locomotives which are relatively new. Some of the locomotives on our run are 30 and 40 years old. The newest ones are all in a major repair program and we are still waiting for the equipment
November 23, 1987

which we were promised. Therefore, the committee is very disappointed in the equipment allocation to the most travelled run. If we are ever going to make money on trains it will be in this corridor.
We are encouraged to hear from VIA that new state-of-the-art F-40 locomotives built at General Motors Diesel in London, Ontario-which is one of the jewels in London- Middlesex-are hopefully going to be added to this line in 1989. This will, no doubt, improve on-time performance.
The senior citizens of Canada are concerned as well. They have told me that they want to travel by train. They live in London and have a family in Toronto, for instance, or they just want to take in the sights. However, no one wants to confront the stairs at Union Station. The stairs are a worrisome obstacle, not only for older people but for parents with baby carriages and for practically anyone with luggage. I hope VIA Rail will install, with the urging of the consultative committee, an escalator in Union Station to make it a little easier to take the train.
The same problem exists for the disabled. They are finding it difficult to use the trains. More people would take the train if the services existed and were advertised.
The consultative committee is encouraged by the improved marketing through joint tourism promotions and advertising which should benefit both the municipality and VIA Rail. However, before the committee gets too involved with increasing ridership, it should understand that they are losing some of their potential customers. It is very important to advertise.
VIA has done this by designating London as the "National Getaway Centre". VIA's computerized reservation system will contain pertinent information on the events taking place in London as well as on hotels, et cetera. VIA reservation clerks and agents will be able to access this information in the computer. This program will be of great benefit to Canadian and American tourists. The City of London is looking forward to the exposure.
If the committees can continue their work and the Minister monitors their reports, we will be able to work together to get a train system which works. The infamous Mussolini made a train system which worked in his country and surely we can do that in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with respect to the question raised by the Hon. Member for London-Middlesex (Mr. Clifford) concerning rail passenger services in southwestern Ontario, I wish to point out first that, as the Minister indicated to the Hon. Member last May, a new consultative committee has been set up by VIA for the London area. It has met and is meeting again this Friday.
Adjournment Debate
I understand that the Hon. Member is part of the committee as well as a member of the North Mainline Route Committee which concerns itself with rail passenger service between Toronto and London through Stratford. If he performs on that committee as he does on the standing committee, I can assure you that he gives the people of that area first-class representation.
I further understand that VIA's fall schedule changes, which are to go into effect on November 29, were the subject of extensive discussions with committee members. As a result of representations from the committees VIA agreed to shift the departure time of the last train on the Toronto-Stratford-London route from 1915 to 1810 to accommodate the needs of most of the users.
A subcommittee of the Northern Mainline Route Committee has been struck to consider marketing, frequency, and further schedule changes. It will report back to the full committee at its next regularly scheduled meeting.
I would like to take this opportunity to comment on the success of new marketing and customer service initiatives that VIA has put in place. A new upgraded VIA-1 first-class service, which was introduced on September 8 throughout the Quebec-Windsor corridor, has met with rave reviews. In midAugust VIA introduced student fares throughout the VIA system after a successful trial.
Because of the renewed commitment to VIA Rail services which the Government announced in May of this year, VIA is able to undertake an extensive program to refurbish VIA's existing equipment which represents a tripling of its budget for such work. This is in addition to the capital investment approved for equipment in terms of the train car modernization program and the acquisition of more new locomotives.
As to the latter, VIA has finished taking delivery for the first order of 30 locomotives at a cost of $75 million. The locomotives were built by General Motors Diesel Division in the city the Hon. Member represents. Contracts for the second order of 26 locomotives are expected to be awarded shortly and GM is one of the firms which will get the contract. VIA is still reviewing its plans for the deployment of the locomotives.
All of these initiatives in respect of equipment, together with the new maintenance facilities, should greatly enhance the reliability and attractiveness of VIA's services.
